cards.title: nice
cards.hook: It began life as an insult.
cards.story: Call someone nice in the 1300s and you had called them a fool. Latin nescius means 'knowing nothing'. It then wandered through timid, fussy and precise before reaching pleasant, and by 1817 Jane Austen was already mocking people for overusing it.
cards.try: The judge drew a nice distinction, in the old sense of very fine and exact.

cards.title: glamour
cards.story: To people who could not read, learning looked like sorcery. So 'grammar' came to mean magic, and in Scots it wore down to glamour, a spell cast on the eyes. Walter Scott made it famous. Every fashion magazine is a grammar book in makeup.
cards.try: The film star's glamour was, in the oldest sense, a spell.

cards.title: bully
cards.hook: It started out as a term of love.
cards.story: In the 1530s a bully was a sweetheart. In A Midsummer Night's Dream, Flute still cries 'O sweet bully Bottom!' Then the word curdled, through 'fine fellow' and 'blusterer', into 'tormentor of the weak' by the 1680s. Love has rarely gone so wrong.
cards.try: When Flute calls him 'sweet bully Bottom', he means dear old Bottom.

cards.title: silly
cards.hook: Once a compliment for the lucky.
cards.story: A thousand years ago, silly meant happy and blessed. Over the centuries it slid to innocent, then pitiable, then foolish. German kept the cousin selig for blissful. English kept the word and lost the bliss.

cards.title: awful
cards.hook: Awe is in it, but no longer.
cards.story: Full of awe: that was awful's whole job, and it was high praise. An awful cathedral made you tremble with wonder. Then people began using the word as mere emphasis, the wonder drained away, and now an awful cathedral just needs repairs.

cards.title: terrific
cards.hook: Its first job was frightening people.
cards.story: Milton gave a serpent a 'hairy mane terrific', and he meant it would scare you stiff. Terrific then softened to mean intense, and then merely great. Today nobody checks a terrific party for snakes.

cards.title: girl
cards.story: In the 1300s a girl could be a boy. Gyrle meant any child or young person, and when Chaucer mentions the 'yonge girles' of a diocese, he means young people of both sexes. Only over later centuries did boys stop being girls.

cards.title: meat
cards.hook: Once it could be a sweet.
cards.story: Old English mete meant any food at all. That is why a sweetmeat is sugary and 'meat and drink' means food and drink. In the King James Bible, the 'meat offering' of Leviticus contains no meat whatsoever: it is made of flour.

cards.title: deer
cards.story: 'Mice and rats, and such small deer' are what Poor Tom lives on in King Lear, and he means exactly that. Old English deor meant any wild animal. Only later did the word settle on the creature with antlers.

cards.title: villain
cards.hook: Every villain started out on a farm.
cards.story: A villain was first a villanus, a labourer on a Roman country estate. Snobbish lords assumed farm workers had bad manners and worse morals, and the word followed their prejudice downhill. Every film villain began as someone's gardener.

cards.title: hussy
cards.story: Hussy is just housewife, worn down by centuries of lazy mouths. It began as a respectful word for the mistress of a house. Slowly it slid downhill into an insult, while housewife, its twin, kept its good name.

cards.title: buxom
cards.story: Buxom comes from bugan, to bend, and for centuries it meant obedient. Medieval brides promised to be 'bonair and buxom' at the altar. It drifted through cheerful and plump before landing on its narrower modern sense.

cards.title: sad
cards.hook: A full stomach started this one.
cards.story: Sad once meant full. Old English sæd was what you felt after a big meal, heavy and done. From full it went to heavy, from heavy to serious, and from serious to sorrowful. Every sad song is, at root, about having had enough.

cards.title: fond
cards.hook: Being fond was once plain stupid.
cards.story: Shakespeare's King Lear calls himself 'a very foolish fond old man', and that fond means foolish too. Middle English fonned meant foolish. Only later did English decide that loving someone a bit foolishly was sweet.

cards.title: clue
cards.story: A clew was a ball of thread. In the Greek myth, Theseus unwinds one to find his way out of the Minotaur's maze. So a clue became anything that leads you through a puzzle. Every detective is still following a piece of string.

cards.title: egregious
cards.origin: Latin e grege, 'out of the flock'
cards.hook: The word once paid you a compliment.
cards.story: Standing out from the flock was praise: Latin e grege gave us a word for someone outstanding. Then, in the late 1500s, people began using egregious sarcastically. The sarcasm won. Today only spectacular blunders are egregious.
cards.try: The report contained one egregious error, repeated in every table.

cards.title: decimate
cards.hook: The Romans did the maths first.
cards.story: A Roman legion that disgraced itself could be decimated: one soldier in every ten chosen by lot and killed by his comrades. Purists still insist the word means a tenth. English disagrees, and uses it to mean nearly all.
cards.try: The first frost decimated the crop, and the purists winced.

cards.title: manufacture
cards.story: Manu factus: made by hand. That is all manufacture ever meant, which is why a robot arm welding a car on a factory floor is doing a job whose name means, quite literally, 'by hand'. Language does not always read the memo.

cards.title: sanguine
cards.hook: Cheerfulness once ran in the blood.
cards.story: Medieval doctors believed your mood came from four body fluids, called humours. Too much blood, or sanguis, made you cheerful and confident. So sanguine means hopeful, although the word still quietly carries the blood.
cards.try: She remained sanguine about the results, even after the first mock.

cards.title: broadcast
cards.hook: Long before radio, farmers did it.
cards.story: To broadcast was to fling seed widely by hand across a field. When radio arrived in the 1920s, engineers borrowed the word: signals scattered in all directions for anyone to catch. Your favourite podcast is, strictly speaking, scattered seed.

cards.title: artificial
cards.hook: St Paul's Cathedral was called this.
cards.story: The story goes that a king told Christopher Wren his new St Paul's was 'awful, amusing and artificial', and Wren was delighted: awe-inspiring, absorbing, full of art. Quote hunters doubt it was ever said, but those were the meanings then.

cards.title: amuse
cards.story: To amuse someone in the 1600s was to distract them, often to deceive them. Armies 'amused' an enemy with a fake attack while the real blow came elsewhere. The pleasant sense came later. Check your wallet after a long magic show.

cards.title: nervous
cards.story: In the 1600s, nervous meant sinewy and strong: nerves were thought of as the body's strings of power, and a 'nervous style' of writing was praised as vigorous. Then nerves became the seat of feeling, and the strong word started to tremble.

cards.title: presently
cards.hook: Now means soon, or now, depending.
cards.story: Presently once meant immediately. Then, like 'just a minute', its promise began to slip, and by the 1600s it could mean 'soon'. In Indian English the present sense lives on: 'presently working in Pune' means right now.

cards.title: prestige
cards.hook: It used to be a conjuring trick.
cards.story: Praestigiae were a conjurer's tricks in Latin, and when prestige arrived in English it meant illusion and deceit. Then people noticed that fame works on us exactly the same way. A prestigious degree is, at root, a dazzling illusion.

cards.title: meticulous
cards.story: Meticulous began as fearful, from Latin metus, 'fear'. In the 1500s a meticulous person was merely timid. Only in the 1800s did it come to mean extremely careful. The idea is honest: the most careful people are often the most scared.
cards.try: He was meticulous about the footnotes, and terrified of the examiner.

cards.title: computer
cards.hook: It used to take a lunch break.
cards.story: From the 1640s, a computer was a person who did sums for a living. NASA's human computers included Katherine Johnson, who checked the numbers for John Glenn's orbit. When the machines arrived, they took both the job and the job title.

cards.title: dashboard
cards.hook: It was there to stop the mud.
cards.story: A dashboard was a wooden board at the front of a horse-drawn carriage. It stopped mud 'dashed' up by the hooves from hitting the driver. Cars kept the name, then apps took it. Every analytics dashboard is, at heart, a mud shield.

cards.title: deadline
cards.hook: It once meant you would be shot.
cards.story: At Andersonville prison in the American Civil War, a line ran inside the stockade. Any prisoner who crossed it could be shot. It was called the dead line. Printers and then newsrooms borrowed the word, and you have been crossing it ever since.

cards.title: cliché
cards.story: Printers called a solid cast metal plate a cliché, probably after the click of the mould hitting hot metal. Its twin was the stereotype. So two of the harshest words for unoriginal thinking come straight from the print shop floor.

cards.title: lord
cards.story: Old English hlafweard: loaf-ward, the keeper of the bread. A lady, hlæfdige, was the kneader of the loaf. In a world where the person who fed you held all the power, a lord was simply the man in charge of the bread bin.

cards.title: husband
cards.hook: It once had nothing to do with marriage.
cards.story: Husband comes from Old Norse hus, house, and bondi, one who dwells or farms. It meant master of a household, married or not. That is why careful farming is husbandry, and a finance minister can husband the nation's money.

cards.title: gossip
cards.hook: Once a solemn promise before God.
cards.story: A godsibb was a godparent, someone spiritually related to your child. Godparents were close friends, and close friends talk. By Shakespeare's day a gossip was a woman's friend at a birth. Soon it was anyone who talked too much.

cards.title: goodbye
cards.story: Say goodbye and you have just squeezed four words into two syllables. 'God be with ye' wore down over time into 'godbwye', and then people, thinking of 'good day', swapped God for good. Every goodbye is a blessing in disguise.

cards.title: school
cards.hook: The Greeks would find this hilarious.
cards.story: School comes from the Greek for leisure. Free time, to an ancient Greek of means, was for debate and learning, so skhole came to mean a place for it. The word for the thing you most want to escape once meant having nothing to do.

cards.title: symposium
cards.story: A Greek symposion was a party where men drank wine, argued and listened to music. Plato set a famous one in his book about love. The word now means an earnest academic meeting, usually with worse drinks.

cards.title: idiot
cards.hook: It once just meant a private citizen.
cards.story: To the Greeks an idiotes was a private person, someone with no public post or special skill. From 'layman' it slid to 'ignorant person', and finally to the insult. It is what an expert means by 'layman', only less polite.

cards.title: hypocrite
cards.hook: It was originally a stage job.
cards.story: Hypokrites was the Greek word for a stage actor. Moralists then noticed that people who pretend to be good are also performing, and the job title became an accusation. Every hypocrite you meet is working without a stage.

cards.title: enthusiasm
cards.story: Greek enthousiasmos meant being possessed by a god: en, in, theos, god. For centuries English used it suspiciously, for religious fanatics. Now it is what a job applicant claims on a CV. The god has left, but the energy stayed.

cards.title: tragedy
cards.story: Tragedy comes from the Greek tragoidia, literally 'goat song'. No one is sure why. Perhaps actors wore goat skins, or a goat was the prize. Whatever the reason, the highest form of Greek theatre is named after a farm animal.

cards.title: disaster
cards.story: A disaster is a badly placed star: dis, bad, and astro, star. Renaissance Italians blamed the planets for shipwrecks and plagues. Astrology faded, but every time a flight is cancelled we still quietly accuse the heavens.

cards.title: consider
cards.hook: You may be looking at the stars.
cards.story: Consider may have begun as 'to observe the stars', from Latin con, with, and sidus, star. Desire is perhaps its cousin, from de sidere, 'from the stars'. Not every scholar agrees, but it is a lovely thought that thinking began by looking up.

cards.title: companion
cards.story: A companion is literally someone you share bread with: com, with, and panis, bread. No promises, no oaths, just a loaf split at the same table. Every company, in the business sense, comes from the same idea.

cards.title: trivial
cards.hook: Grammar is part of the reason.
cards.story: Latin trivium means 'where three roads meet', the place for street-corner gossip. It also named the first three subjects of medieval school: grammar, logic and rhetoric. Either way, trivial meant common. The CAT verbal section is, strictly, trivial.

cards.title: cattle
cards.story: Cattle, chattel and capital are one word, all from Latin caput, 'head', by way of 'property'. Old English feoh, cattle, became fee. Latin pecu, cattle, gave us pecuniary. Your bank balance is, at root, a herd.

cards.title: candidate
cards.story: Roman candidates wore togas rubbed with chalk so they looked spotlessly white and therefore honest. Latin candidus, white, is also where candid comes from. Election posters have always been in the business of bleaching.

cards.title: muscle
cards.hook: Flex your arm and look closely.
cards.story: Latin musculus means 'little mouse', because a flexing bicep was thought to look like a small mouse running under the skin. Bodybuilders are spending their whole lives cultivating an impressive collection of mice.

cards.title: daisy
cards.hook: Say it slowly. It is a poem.
cards.story: Old English dæges eage: the day's eye. The flower closes at night and opens at dawn, like an eye waking up. Someone looked at a lawn a thousand years ago and named it with more poetry than most of us manage in a lifetime.

cards.title: fathom
cards.story: A fathom was once the span of your two outstretched arms, roughly six feet. Sailors measured depth that way. From measuring water it came to mean getting to the bottom of anything. If you cannot fathom something, you cannot get your arms round it.

cards.title: sarcasm
cards.story: Greek sarkazein meant to tear flesh, as dogs do. It came to mean speaking bitterly, as though biting. Sarcasm, in the literal sense, is when the words draw blood. Anyone with a sharp-tongued aunt will know this is accurate.

cards.title: bead
cards.story: Old English gebed meant a prayer. When you told your beads on a rosary, you were counting your prayers. Slowly the word slid from the prayers to the small round things used to count them. Every bead necklace is, at root, a prayer.

cards.title: shampoo
cards.story: Shampoo comes from Hindi champo, 'knead', and began as a massage. Sake Dean Mahomed, from Patna, brought it to Regency Brighton and became Shampooing Surgeon to George IV and William IV. The hair-washing meaning came decades later.

cards.title: pyjamas
cards.story: Paijama means 'leg garment', and in India they were ordinary daytime trousers. British men adopted them for lounging and bed, and carried the idea home. So the rest of the world ended up sleeping in what Indians wore to work.

cards.title: bungalow
cards.hook: The house is named after a region.
cards.story: A bangla was a low, single-storey house in the Bengali style, with a thatched roof and a wide veranda. British officials copied it across India and then at seaside resorts back home. England's suburbs are dotted with small tributes to Bengal.

cards.title: veranda
cards.story: Portuguese sailors had varanda, Hindi speakers had varanda, and nobody is sure who had it first. British officers sat on it, drank on it and carried it home. The argument continues, preferably in the shade.

cards.title: jungle
cards.story: Sanskrit jangala meant dry, scrubby, uncultivated land. In Hindi, jangal meant any wild country. British writers attached it to India's dense forests, and the meaning changed sides. The rainforest's name once meant 'almost a desert'.

cards.title: loot
cards.hook: A word that came home with the Company.
cards.story: Hindi lut meant plunder. The historian William Dalrymple calls loot one of the very first Indian words to enter English, and it spread in the late 1700s, just as East India Company fortunes were coming home. Some words arrive with the goods.

cards.title: thug
cards.hook: A word with a contested history.
cards.story: Thag was the Hindi word for a swindler. In the 1830s, British officials announced a secret brotherhood of stranglers on India's highways, and thug went global. Historians now argue the British exaggerated them, but the word never left.

cards.title: juggernaut
cards.hook: A word built from a missionary tale.
cards.story: Jagannatha, 'lord of the world', is honoured at Puri with giant chariots pulled through the streets. British missionaries spread lurid tales of worshippers crushed under the wheels, and the word juggernaut rolled into English on those stories.
cards.try: The new tax law rolled on like a juggernaut, flattening every objection.

cards.title: cot
cards.story: The simple Indian rope bed, the khat or charpai, gave British homes the word cot. Hindi khat goes back to Sanskrit khatva. So the crib in a Surrey nursery and the string bed on a Punjabi roof are, etymologically, the same piece of furniture.

cards.title: dinghy
cards.story: Dingi was a small rowing boat on Indian rivers. In English the spelling picked up an h, so nobody would read the g soft, as in dingy. Most English spelling is careless. This one letter was added on purpose.

cards.title: catamaran
cards.hook: The design is in the name.
cards.story: Kattu means to tie and maram means wood. The Tamil kattumaram was simply logs lashed together. Yachts costing millions still carry its name and, in essence, its idea.

cards.title: mulligatawny
cards.story: Milagu thanni is Tamil for 'pepper water', a close relative of rasam. British officers in Madras asked for soup, and Tamil cooks obliged. Victorian dining rooms then served a fashionable soup whose name meant, plainly, pepper water.

cards.title: curry
cards.story: Curry comes from Tamil kari, 'sauce'. The Forme of Cury, a cookbook of about 1390, is unrelated: that 'cury' is a French-derived word for cooking. The first curry recipe printed in English came in 1747, spiced with nothing but pepper and coriander.

cards.title: cash
cards.story: Cash is really two words that collided. Cash the money comes from French caisse, a money box. But the small coins of India and China were also called cash, from Tamil kasu. Say 'cash' and you are speaking two languages at once.

cards.title: teak
cards.hook: The Royal Navy sailed on Malayalam.
cards.story: Teak reached English through the Portuguese, from Malayalam tekka. The wood is so oily that it barely rots. HMS Trincomalee, a Royal Navy frigate built of teak in Bombay by the Wadia shipbuilders in 1817, is still afloat today, in Hartlepool.

cards.title: avatar
cards.story: Sanskrit avatara means a descent, especially a god coming down to earth in bodily form. In the 1980s computer game designers borrowed the word for your on-screen self. Technically, whenever you log in you are a deity who has condescended to appear.

cards.title: guru
cards.story: Guru comes from the Sanskrit for heavy: a teacher is a person of weight. Latin gravis, 'heavy', is its cousin, giving us grave and gravity. So when you touch a guru's feet, you are honouring the same idea that keeps them on the floor.

cards.title: nirvana
cards.hook: The peace of a candle going out.
cards.story: Nirvana does not quite mean bliss. It means 'blowing out', as of a flame: nir, out, and va, to blow. In Buddhist thought the fires of desire and suffering go out. The highest state of peace is named after a candle being extinguished.

cards.title: karma
cards.hook: It is about doing, not fate.
cards.story: Karma is not fate. It means action, from Sanskrit karman, the deed you do. The idea is that actions carry consequences. English has turned it into a cosmic vending machine, but the original word is about your own doing.

cards.title: yoga
cards.hook: Your yoga mat knows about oxen.
cards.story: Yoga comes from Sanskrit yuj, to yoke, as oxen are yoked to a plough. English yoke is its direct cousin, as are junction and join. The next time someone calls a yoga class relaxing, tell them it is named after farm equipment.

cards.title: mantra
cards.story: Mantra joins man, to think, with tra, instrument. It is literally a tool for thinking, and its root is the same as English mind and mental. A corporate mantra, repeated in every meeting, may not be what the ancient sages had in mind.

cards.title: pundit
cards.story: A pandita was a scholar trained in Sanskrit learning and law, and British India used the term for learned advisers. In modern English a pundit is someone on television with strong opinions. The learning is, in many cases, optional.

cards.title: pariah
cards.hook: A word to handle with care.
cards.story: Paraiyar is the name of a Tamil community, long linked to the parai drum. European writers turned it into an English word for outcast, a prejudice frozen in vocabulary. Many now avoid using it lightly. Knowing where it came from is part of why.

cards.title: sugar
cards.story: Sanskrit sharkara meant grit or gravel, which is what the first sugar crystals looked like. It travelled through Persian and Arabic to become sugar, and through Malayalam and Portuguese to become jaggery. The two words are one word, separated at birth.

cards.title: orange
cards.hook: It lost its n on the way.
cards.story: It began as Sanskrit naranga, then became Persian narang and Arabic naranj. In Italian, una narancia was misheard as un' arancia, and the n vanished. Before the fruit arrived, English had no single word for the colour, which is why robins have 'red' breasts.

cards.title: mango
cards.hook: Some Americans think it is a pepper.
cards.story: Tamil mankay became Portuguese manga and English mango. Mangoes reached cold countries pickled, so mango seems to have come to mean 'a pickle', and a stuffed pickled pepper was 'a mango'. In parts of the American Midwest, a green pepper is still called one.

cards.title: chutney
cards.hook: It tells you how to eat it.
cards.story: Chatni comes from chatna, to lick. British cooks took it home as a sweet fruity relish, but the name still tells you how it was meant to be eaten. The Hindi word is also the best review any food has ever had.

cards.title: pepper
cards.hook: It beat the Raj by a thousand years.
cards.story: Long before the Raj, even before the Normans, English had the word pepper, borrowed from Latin, from Greek, from Sanskrit pippali. The Indian spice trade had reached Old English kitchens a thousand years before the East India Company.

cards.title: ginger
cards.story: Sanskrit called ginger shringavera, 'horn-bodied', which sounds perfect for the knobbly root. But scholars suspect that is a clever reshaping of a southern word, Tamil inji ver, 'ginger root'. The English spice may wear a Sanskrit mask over a Tamil face.

cards.title: kedgeree
cards.hook: The full English that is not.
cards.story: Khichri is rice and lentils cooked together, comfort food across India. British officers fell for it, added smoked fish and eggs, and took it home. Kedgeree became a Victorian breakfast staple. It is khichdi that went to boarding school.

cards.title: chintz
cards.story: Indian printed cotton, chhint, was so popular in England that weavers rioted and Parliament banned it, in the Calico Acts of 1700 and 1721. Chintzy now means cheap, but the cloth's original crime was being too beautiful to compete with.

cards.title: calico
cards.story: Calico is named after Calicut, now Kozhikode, the Kerala port that shipped cotton cloth to the world. Americans even call a patchy three-coloured cat a calico, after the printed cloth. An Ohio cat, in a sense, is dressed from Malabar.

cards.title: dungarees
cards.story: Dungri was a coarse blue cotton cloth, and its name is usually traced to Dongri, a dockside village that is now part of Mumbai. Sailors and labourers wore it. The overalls in a trendy coffee shop may be quoting a street in Mumbai.

cards.title: khaki
cards.story: Khak is Persian and Urdu for dust. In 1848 the Corps of Guides on the North-West Frontier took up uniforms the colour of the ground. Soldiers everywhere followed. Every army in dust-coloured uniform is wearing a word that means dirt.

cards.title: jodhpurs
cards.story: Sir Pratap Singh of Jodhpur perfected these loose-topped, close-calved riding trousers. In 1897, at Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee, his polo team stunned London in them. British riders copied the style, and the word followed the trousers home.

cards.title: cummerbund
cards.story: Kamar means waist and band means band. A cummerbund is a waistband, literally, and British officers in India wore them before London's tailors took them up. Now every black-tie dinner features a small strip of Urdu across the middle.

cards.title: bandanna
cards.hook: The dye trick is in the name.
cards.story: Bandhna means to tie, and it names tie-dyeing, the Indian craft of knotting cloth so that dye leaves patterns. Its cousin, bandhani, is still made in Gujarat and Rajasthan. Cowboys eventually wore the word around their necks.

cards.title: seersucker
cards.story: Shir o shakar means 'milk and sugar': the smooth and the rough in one cloth, with flat stripes and puckered ones. The poetic name came through India into English as seersucker. A summer suit in Boston is, quite literally, wearing a dessert.

cards.title: gymkhana
cards.hook: It has nothing to do with the gym.
cards.story: Gend-khana meant a ball-court. The British in India thought the first half sounded like 'gym', changed the spelling, and gave the word to sports clubs. Every gymkhana in India is a small monument to a spelling mistake.

cards.title: pukka
cards.story: Pakka means cooked or ripe, the opposite of kachcha, raw. It came to mean solid, proper, the real thing. Colonial Britons spoke of a pukka sahib. Then Jamie Oliver, the Essex chef, made 'pukka' his catchword and took it round the world.

cards.title: cushy
cards.hook: The trenches learnt it from India.
cards.story: Khush is Persian and Hindi for pleasant. British soldiers in India took it up, and during the First World War a 'cushy' job meant a safe one far from the front. It has no connection to cushions, though it is very happy to let you think so.

cards.title: doolally
cards.hook: A real place that drove men mad.
cards.story: Deolali, near Nashik, was the British Army's transit camp where soldiers waited for ships home, sometimes for months, in heat and boredom. Men who cracked had 'doolally tap', tap being fever. To go doolally is to lose your mind near Nashik.

cards.title: Blighty
cards.hook: Britain's pet name for itself is Indian.
cards.story: Vilayati meant foreign, and Indians used it for British goods and British people. Soldiers twisted it to Blighty and used it, with deep longing, for home. England's most sentimental nickname for itself means, in Hindustani, 'abroad'.

cards.title: dekko
cards.story: Dekho is the Hindi command 'look!'. British soldiers, who heard it endlessly, took it home, and 'have a dekko' became respectable British slang for 'take a look'. A Hindi imperative is still giving orders in English pubs.

cards.title: bandicoot
cards.story: Pandi-kokku is Telugu for 'pig-rat', the large rodent of Indian grain stores. When Europeans reached Australia and saw a pointy-nosed marsupial, they called it a bandicoot too. The real bandicoot is in India. The famous one is a lookalike.

cards.title: mongoose
cards.hook: It has nothing to do with geese.
cards.story: From Marathi mungus, and Dravidian before that, mongoose got its spelling from English ears that heard a goose in it. So the plural is mongooses, not mongeese. Rikki-Tikki-Tavi, at least, was never once mistaken for poultry.

cards.title: cheetah
cards.story: Cheetah comes from Hindi chita, from Sanskrit chitrakaya, 'with a speckled body'. The same chitra, bright or spotted, gave us chintz. So the fastest animal on land and your grandmother's flowery curtains are cousins, joined by their spots.

cards.title: anaconda
cards.story: The world's heaviest snake lives in South America, but its name probably comes from Sri Lanka: Sinhala henakandaya, 'whip snake', or Tamil anaikondran, 'elephant-killer'. A naturalist's mix-up seems to have moved the name across the world.

cards.title: punch
cards.story: Five ingredients: alcohol, sugar, lemon, water and spice. That, runs the old story, is why Hindi panch, 'five', named the drink. But nobody has found panch used for a drink in India, and the English word may come from puncheon, a cask.

cards.title: toddy
cards.hook: A Scottish cure, made in India.
cards.story: Hot toddy, Scotland's famous cure for a winter cold, is named after Hindi tari, the fermenting sap of the palmyra palm. Indian palm juice gave the word. Scottish whisky took the credit, and a grateful world took the honey and lemon.

cards.title: tank
cards.hook: India gave it. A war code name stuck.
cards.story: Tank came through Portuguese from Gujarati or Marathi, meaning a water cistern. In 1915 the British, building a secret armoured vehicle, told everyone it was a water carrier. They called it a tank for cover, and the disguise stuck.

cards.title: pal
cards.hook: A very long walk to your mate.
cards.story: Romani speakers, whose ancestors left India around a thousand years ago, carried Sanskrit bhratr, 'brother', west as phral, and English borrowed it as pal. So your pal is a Sanskrit brother who walked to England the long way round.

cards.title: polo
cards.story: Polo is the Balti word for ball. Tea planters in Assam learnt the game from Manipuri players in the 1850s, and the world's oldest surviving polo club was founded in Calcutta in 1862. The sport of kings comes with a Himalayan ball.

cards.title: zen
cards.hook: A Sanskrit word in Japanese clothes.
cards.story: Sanskrit dhyana, meditation, became Chinese chan and then Japanese zen. A word for sitting still crossed half of Asia over a thousand years, changing its pronunciation at every border. The calmest word in English is one of its most travelled.

cards.title: brilliant
cards.hook: Brilliance may have a home town.
cards.story: Beryl, a green gemstone, probably takes its name from a south Indian town, Velur, through Prakrit and Greek. Italian made a verb, brillare, 'to sparkle like beryl', and English got brilliant. So brilliance may have a birthplace in south India.

cards.title: lakh
cards.hook: A bug may have taught India to count.
cards.story: Lac, the resin behind lacquer and shellac, is made by insects in enormous swarms. Sanskrit laksha means both the resin and one hundred thousand. One old story says the number came from the swarms. Scholars are not sure, but the idea is irresistible.

cards.title: crimson
cards.hook: The colour of a crushed insect.
cards.story: Crimson dye came from crushed kermes insects, and the word travelled from Sanskrit krmi, worm, through Persian and Arabic qirmiz. Carmine comes from the same source. Every crimson rose in every poem owes its colour word to an insect.

cards.title: indigo
cards.story: Greek indikon simply meant 'the Indian stuff', and it named the deep blue dye Europe had to import from India. Indigo farming in Bengal later caused such misery that peasants revolted in 1859. Some beautiful words have hard histories.

cards.title: tamarind
cards.hook: Arab traders called it a date.
cards.story: Arabic tamr hindi means 'Indian date', which is what traders took the sticky brown pod to be. Medieval Latin made it tamarindus, and English tamarind followed. Your imli chutney is named after a very old case of mistaken fruit identity.

cards.title: lilac
cards.hook: Through Persia to the English garden.
cards.story: Sanskrit nila means dark blue (the Nilgiri hills are the 'blue mountains'). Persian made nilak, bluish, then lilak, and Arabic and French passed it on. The pale English lilac bush takes its name from a Sanskrit word for deep blue.

cards.title: musk
cards.story: Musk, the prized base of many perfumes, comes through Persian and Greek from Sanskrit muska, literally 'little mouse', a name probably inspired by the shape of the musk deer's scent gland. Your expensive perfume may owe its name to a very small mouse.

cards.title: mandarin
cards.hook: It was never a Chinese word.
cards.story: Mandarin is not a Chinese word. It comes from Sanskrit mantrin, 'minister', the same word as Hindi mantri. Portuguese traders took it from Malay and applied it to Chinese officials. So your local mantri and the mandarins of Beijing share a job title.

cards.title: rupee
cards.story: Rupee goes back to Sanskrit rupya, worked or stamped silver. Sher Shah Suri issued the silver rupiya in the 1540s, and the coin outlived empires: it was still the model for British India's money. Every rupee note in your wallet has a Sanskrit silver lining.

cards.title: mother
cards.hook: A Calcutta judge spotted the family.
cards.story: In 1786 Sir William Jones, a judge in Calcutta, told scholars that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin were too alike to be accidental: they must share a lost common source. Matr and mater, pitr and pater, bhratr and brother. English was Sanskrit's long-lost cousin.

cards.title: video
cards.story: Sanskrit veda, knowledge, and Latin videre, to see, grew from the same ancient root, because to know something is to have seen it. That root also gave English wit, wise, vision and idea. Veda and video are, at root, the same thought: seeing is knowing.

cards.title: Jupiter
cards.story: Jupiter comes from Latin Iuppiter, 'sky father'. The Rigveda has Dyaus Pita, also 'sky father'. Same words, same idea, from a language older than both. A Roman priest and a Vedic poet were, without knowing it, calling on the same family god.

cards.title: hibernate
cards.story: Himalaya is Sanskrit for 'abode of snow', from hima, snow. Latin hiems, winter, is hima's ancient cousin, and gave us hibernate. A bear dozing in Canada is, etymologically, doing what the Himalayas do: being full of winter.

cards.title: chess
cards.story: Chess began in India as chaturanga, 'four limbs', the four divisions of an ancient army: foot soldiers, cavalry, elephants and chariots. Persia adopted the game, Arabic reshaped it, and the elephant eventually became the bishop. Knights still move like horses.

cards.title: Moksha Patam
cards.story: Long before it reached Victorian nurseries, Snakes and Ladders was an Indian game about liberation, with ladders for virtues and snakes for vices. The snakes outnumbered the ladders. English makers kept the game and evened up the odds.

cards.title: almirah
cards.hook: Not an Indian word at all.
cards.story: Almirah sounds Indian and lives in Indian homes, but it came to India from Portuguese armario, a cupboard. So did the pav in vada pav, from pao, bread. Mumbai's favourite snack has been speaking Portuguese all along.

cards.title: prepone
cards.hook: India fixed a gap in English.
cards.story: English had postpone but no one-word opposite, so India supplied one: prepone, to move something earlier. Oxford's dictionaries now include it. The word flickered in older English writing, but India is where it came alive. Schedulers everywhere owe India one.
cards.try: The exam has been preponed to Monday, so revise tonight.

cards.title: do the needful
cards.hook: An old office phrase that stayed.
cards.story: To 'do the needful' sounds purely Indian, but it turns up in older British writing too, and clerks of the Raj may well have used it. Britain let it fade. India's offices kept it alive. Yesterday's Victorian phrase is today's Bengaluru email.
cards.try: Kindly do the needful and revert by end of day.

cards.title: your good name
cards.story: When someone asks 'What is your good name?', they are politely translating Hindi shubh naam, 'auspicious name'. It sounds odd to British ears, but then 'How do you do?' is not a genuine question either. Manners rarely translate word for word.

cards.title: atoll
cards.hook: A Maldivian word in every atlas.
cards.story: Dhivehi, the language of the Maldives, gave English very few words, but atoll is one of them. Charles Darwin used it to explain how coral reefs grow, and now the entire world uses the Maldivian word for a ring of coral.

cards.title: Bombay duck
cards.hook: It is a fish, and nobody knows why.
cards.story: Bombay duck is a small dried fish, the bombil. No duck has ever been involved. One old story blames the Bombay mail, the dak, whose smell the fish shared. Nobody has proved it, and the fish does not care.

cards.title: India ink
cards.story: The black ink the world calls India ink was invented in China. The name comes from trade: the ink or its materials often reached Europe through India. The French, more honestly, call it encre de Chine, Chinese ink. Centuries of wrong directions.

cards.title: India
cards.hook: How a river became a nation.
cards.story: India is named after the Indus. Sanskrit Sindhu means 'river'. Persian speakers turned the s to h, giving Hindu, and the Greeks dropped the h, giving Indos and India. A simple word for 'river' became the name of a civilisation.

cards.title: godown
cards.hook: Nothing to do with going down.
cards.story: Indian English calls a warehouse a godown, and it has nothing to do with going down stairs. It comes from Malay gudang, itself from Tamil kidangu or Telugu gidangi, a storeroom. The word went to Malaya and came back home in disguise.

cards.title: compound
cards.hook: Your society wall may be Malay.
cards.story: The 'compound' around an Indian house has nothing to do with the chemistry word. It probably comes from Malay kampung, a village or enclosure, via Portuguese or Dutch traders. The compound wall you grew up behind may be a small piece of Malay.

cards.title: nabob
cards.hook: London sneered at its new rich.
cards.story: A nawab was a Mughal provincial governor. Britons who returned from India with huge fortunes were sneered at as nabobs: rich, vulgar and suspiciously sunburnt. Samuel Foote mocked them on stage in 1772. An Indian title ended up as an English insult.

cards.title: mogul
cards.story: Mughal is the Persian word for Mongol, and the dynasty claimed descent from Genghis Khan. Their vast wealth made the word mean 'great personage' in English. Hollywood's movie moguls were named after the emperors of Agra, whether they knew it or not.

cards.title: sandwich
cards.hook: A lord who would not leave the table.
cards.story: The 4th Earl of Sandwich, runs the story, asked for meat between bread so he could keep playing cards. Others say it was so he could keep working at his desk. Either way, one of Britain's great noble titles survives mainly as a lunch.

cards.title: boycott
cards.hook: One man's name, one Irish village.
cards.story: Captain Charles Boycott was a land agent in County Mayo who tried to evict tenants in 1880. The whole community simply stopped speaking to him, serving him and working for him. Within weeks his name had become a verb, and it has never stopped.
cards.try: Students voted to boycott the canteen until prices fell.

cards.title: guillotine
cards.hook: He did not invent it or die by it.
cards.story: Dr Guillotin argued that execution should be painless and equal, but he did not invent the machine and was not killed by it. He died in bed in 1814. His family reportedly begged France to rename the device, then changed their own name instead.

cards.title: silhouette
cards.hook: A name for doing things on the cheap.
cards.story: Étienne de Silhouette served France as finance minister in 1759, and his harsh cost-cutting made 'a la Silhouette' a sneer meaning cheap. Black paper profiles were the budget alternative to real portraits, so the minister, it seems, gave them his name.

cards.title: mesmerise
cards.hook: He healed with an invisible fluid.
cards.story: Franz Mesmer, an 18th-century doctor, claimed an invisible fluid flowed through all bodies and could be steered by a healer. Benjamin Franklin sat on the French commission that found it was all imagination. Mesmer's reward is a word for being spellbound.

cards.title: galvanise
cards.story: In the 1780s, Luigi Galvani made dead frogs' legs twitch with electricity. His name became a verb meaning to shock something into action. Steel can also be galvanised, which is the same idea applied with a much more boring result.
cards.try: The defeat galvanised the team into a month of early mornings.

cards.title: maverick
cards.hook: A rancher who wouldn't brand cows.
cards.story: Samuel Maverick, a Texas rancher in the 1800s, left his cattle unbranded. Stray, unmarked cattle came to be called mavericks, and the name moved on to humans who refuse to follow the herd. His grandson later coined gobbledygook. It runs in the family.

cards.title: bowdlerise
cards.hook: His sister did most of the cutting.
cards.story: Thomas Bowdler's Family Shakespeare cut everything unfit for a lady's ears, and his name became the verb for censoring. But the first edition, in 1807, was largely the work of his sister Henrietta, who left her name off. She escaped the infamy.

cards.title: dunce
cards.hook: Named after a genius, on purpose.
cards.story: John Duns Scotus was one of the subtlest thinkers of the Middle Ages. His followers so annoyed Renaissance humanists that 'Dunsman' became an insult for a dull pedant, and then dunce. One of history's finest minds now stands in the corner.

cards.title: maudlin
cards.hook: Oxford still says it this way.
cards.story: Medieval paintings showed Mary Magdalene forever weeping, so her name, said 'maudlin' in English, came to mean tearfully sentimental. Oxford's Magdalen College still says it that way. A saint's tears became English's word for soppy self-pity.

cards.title: gerrymander
cards.hook: A governor, a salamander, a map.
cards.story: In 1812, Massachusetts Governor Elbridge Gerry signed a bill carving election districts for party gain. One district looked so twisted that a cartoonist gave it claws and a tail: the Gerry-mander. Gerry said his name with a hard G, which nobody remembers.

cards.title: shrapnel
cards.hook: It was named after a lieutenant.
cards.story: Henry Shrapnel, a British artillery officer, invented a hollow shell packed with musket balls in the 1780s. It burst in the air and showered the enemy. The army used it against Napoleon, and its inventor's name has been falling from the sky ever since.

cards.title: mentor
cards.story: In the Odyssey, Mentor is the old friend asked to look after Odysseus's son. But at crucial moments it is really the goddess Athena, disguised as Mentor, who gives the advice. So the word for a wise guide is named after a case of divine impersonation.

cards.title: martinet
cards.story: Jean Martinet drilled Louis XIV's French army into the model of a modern professional force, and soldiers obeyed out of fear. His name entered English for anyone obsessed with rules. He was killed in 1672 at a siege, reportedly by his own side's fire.
cards.try: The new principal was a martinet about shoelaces.

cards.title: chauvinist
cards.story: Nicolas Chauvin was Napoleon's most fanatically loyal soldier, wounded seventeen times, or so French plays claimed. Historians have found no trace of him. A probably fictional super-patriot gave his name to real blind loyalty.

cards.title: Luddite
cards.hook: He may never have smashed anything.
cards.story: In the 1810s English weavers smashed machines that threatened their wages, signing letters from 'General Ludd'. Ned Ludd was probably mythical. Today Luddite insults anyone who is bad with phones, which is unfair to skilled craftsmen who had a point.

cards.title: derrick
cards.hook: A crane named after an executioner.
cards.story: Thomas Derrick was the hangman at Tyburn around 1600, and his gallows was a beam with pulleys. His name passed to any such hoisting frame, and then to the cranes on oil rigs. Next time you see a derrick, think about what it was first for.

cards.title: salmonella
cards.hook: It has no connection to fish.
cards.story: Salmonella is not named after salmon. It is named after Daniel Salmon, an American vet whose assistant Theobald Smith actually found the germ. Smith did the work, Salmon's name went on it, and the fish has been taking the blame ever since.

cards.title: bougainvillea
cards.hook: The woman who found it was disguised.
cards.story: Bougainvillea, blazing over Indian walls, is named after a French admiral. But Jeanne Baret, dressed as a man to join his voyage, probably helped collect it. She became the first woman known to sail round the world. The admiral got the flower.

cards.title: algorithm
cards.hook: Your feed is named after him.
cards.story: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, a scholar in 9th-century Baghdad, wrote the book that taught Europe Indian numerals. His name, Latinised as Algoritmi, became algorithm. Every time your feed shows you something, it is honouring a Persian mathematician.

cards.title: Bluetooth
cards.hook: A Viking king is in your earbuds.
cards.story: King Harald Bluetooth united Denmark's tribes in the 900s. In 1997 an engineer proposed his nickname for a technology that would unite devices. The logo is built from the runes for H and B, so your earbuds are wearing a Viking's initials.

cards.title: boson
cards.hook: One family of particles has a Bengali name.
cards.story: All particles are either fermions or bosons. In 1924, Satyendra Nath Bose, teaching in Dhaka, sent Einstein a paper that reshaped physics. Paul Dirac named one entire family of particles bosons in his honour, and that includes the Higgs.

cards.title: Hobson's choice
cards.hook: Pick any horse, as long as it is this one.
cards.story: Thomas Hobson hired out horses in Cambridge around 1600 and insisted you take the one nearest the stable door or go without. Milton wrote poems about him. A choice with only one option is still, four hundred years on, named after him.
cards.try: With one centre left in the city, it was Hobson's choice.

cards.title: guy
cards.hook: Every 'you guys' is a bomb plot.
cards.story: Guy Fawkes failed to blow up Parliament in 1605, and effigies of him, called guys, were burned every November. A 'guy' came to mean a strangely dressed person, then any man. Every time you say 'you guys', you are quoting a failed bomber.

cards.title: teddy bear
cards.hook: A president refused to shoot it.
cards.story: On a 1902 hunting trip in Mississippi, President Theodore Roosevelt refused to shoot a bear tied to a tree. A cartoon appeared, a toymaker asked permission, and 'Teddy's bear' was born. One act of sporting restraint became the most cuddled toy on earth.

cards.title: sideburns
cards.story: American Civil War general Ambrose Burnside wore startling whiskers joined to his moustache, and they were called burnsides. Someone swapped the halves and they became sideburns, which at least made sense, because they grow on the side.

cards.title: nicotine
cards.story: Jean Nicot, French ambassador to Portugal, sent tobacco to Paris around 1560 as a wonder drug. A plant that later killed millions was named in honour of the diplomat who promoted it as medicine. His memorial is every cigarette warning.

cards.title: saxophone
cards.story: Adolphe Sax, a Belgian instrument maker, patented the saxophone in 1846. As a child he reportedly fell from a height, swallowed a needle and was nearly poisoned, and neighbours called him 'little Sax, the ghost'. Jazz, you could say, got very lucky.

cards.title: leotard
cards.hook: The daring young man wore this.
cards.story: Jules Léotard invented the flying trapeze act in 1859 and wore a tight one-piece to show off his muscles and stay clear of the ropes. A song of the time immortalised him as the 'daring young man on the flying trapeze'. Gymnasts have worn his name ever since.

cards.title: cardigan
cards.story: The 7th Earl of Cardigan led the Light Brigade into disaster at Balaclava in 1854. His men wore a button-front knitted waistcoat, and the knitted balaclava is named after the same battle. Britain's cosiest winter clothes came out of a catastrophe.

cards.title: diesel
cards.story: Rudolf Diesel patented his engine in the 1890s. In 1913 he boarded a steamer for England and vanished in the night. A body found at sea days later was identified by his belongings. The mystery was never solved, but every diesel truck still carries his name.

cards.title: mausoleum
cards.story: King Mausolus ruled a corner of Asia Minor. His widow built him a tomb so magnificent at Halicarnassus that it became a wonder of the ancient world. Every grand tomb since has been called a mausoleum, including the Taj Mahal.

cards.title: tantalise
cards.story: Tantalus, in Greek myth, stands in water with fruit above his head, and both retreat when he reaches for them. English made a verb of him. Every discount email and every almost-solved puzzle is a small tribute to his eternal frustration.

cards.title: panic
cards.story: Pan, the Greek god of the wild, was said to fill lonely travellers with sudden, groundless terror. Greeks called it panikos, 'of Pan'. Every panic attack and panic buy is, by name, the work of a goat-legged god who enjoyed scaring people.

cards.title: pants
cards.story: Pantalone was a skinny old miser in Italian comedy, wearing long tight leggings. His name became pantaloons, then pants. Pantalone was probably named after St Pantaleon, popular in Venice. Your trousers are, by a roundabout route, a saint.

cards.title: hooligan
cards.hook: A surname from the music hall.
cards.story: In the 1890s, London police courts began reporting gangs called the Hooligans. The name was probably a comic Irish surname from the music halls. A stereotype of the day hardened into a word that now appears in headlines from Mumbai to Moscow.

cards.title: cereal
cards.story: Ceres was the Roman goddess of grain and the harvest. Her name gives us cereal, so every box on your kitchen shelf is named after a goddess whom a Roman farmer would have prayed to for a good crop.

cards.title: jovial
cards.hook: Your mood was the planets' fault.
cards.story: Astrologers believed being born under a planet shaped you. Jove, or Jupiter, made you jolly, Saturn made you gloomy, Mercury made you quick. English kept them all: jovial, saturnine, mercurial. Astronomy fired the planets, but the adjectives kept the job.

cards.title: Braille
cards.story: Louis Braille lost his sight at three, after an accident with an awl in his father's workshop. At fifteen he invented a code of raised dots, punched out with a stylus not unlike that awl. The kind of tool that took his sight gave reading to millions.

cards.title: quisling
cards.story: Vidkun Quisling helped Nazi Germany take over Norway in 1940 and ruled as a puppet leader. He was shot for treason in 1945. The Times was using his name as a noun for traitor within days of the invasion: infamy at unusual speed.

cards.title: spoonerism
cards.hook: His most famous slips are fakes.
cards.story: The Reverend William Spooner of Oxford was famous for swapping sounds, as in 'a blushing crow' for 'a crushing blow'. But the Oxford Dictionary of Quotations could confirm only one real example. Almost all the classics were invented by his delighted students.

cards.title: gun
cards.hook: It probably began as a woman's name.
cards.story: A 1330s inventory at Windsor Castle lists a huge crossbow named Domina Gunilda, Lady Gunhilda. Weapons were often given women's names, and gunne probably comes from hers. Every gun ever fired has, quite possibly, been named after a lady.

cards.title: alcohol
cards.hook: Your eyeliner and your whisky are related.
cards.story: Arabic al-kuhl was kohl, the fine black powder used to line the eyes. Alchemists used the word for any refined essence, then for the essence of wine. So the kohl around an eye and the whisky in a glass are the very same word.

cards.title: algebra
cards.story: Al-jabr, in the title of al-Khwarizmi's famous 9th-century book, means 'the restoring of broken parts'. In Spain, an algebrista was a bone-setter, often the barber. When you balance an equation you are, in the old sense, setting a broken leg.

cards.title: zero
cards.story: Indian mathematicians called nothing shunya, 'empty'. Arab scholars translated it as sifr. Italian turned sifr into zero, while English also kept cipher. One Arabic word, carrying a Sanskrit idea, gave us both nothing and the secret code.

cards.title: admiral
cards.story: Arabic amir al-bahr meant 'commander of the sea'. Europeans grabbed the first bit, amir-al, and thought that was the whole title. So every admiral's title is, more or less, the words 'commander of', with the sea left out.

cards.title: assassin
cards.story: Medieval enemies of the Nizari Ismailis called them hashishiyyin, hashish-eaters, as an insult. Marco Polo's lurid tales spread it, and the word became assassin. Historians find little evidence the group actually used the drug. A slander became a word.

cards.title: safari
cards.story: Arabic safar, 'journey', came into Swahili as safari and then into English through East Africa. Hindi also took safar for journey. So a Hindi speaker on a safar and a British tourist on safari are using the same Arabic word.

cards.title: magazine
cards.story: Makhazin is Arabic for storehouses, and a magazine first meant a warehouse for goods or gunpowder. An English editor in 1731 called his miscellany The Gentleman's Magazine, a storehouse of knowledge. A gun's magazine remembers the older sense.

cards.title: arsenal
cards.hook: Less about guns, more about making.
cards.story: Arabic dar as-sina'a meant 'house of making', a workshop. Venice took the word for its shipyard, the Arsenale, and it drifted to mean a store of weapons. A north London football club is now named after an Arabic word for a factory.

cards.title: mattress
cards.story: Matrah is Arabic for a place where something is thrown, and that something was a cushion on the floor. Europeans, who slept on straw, adopted both the idea and the word. Your expensive orthopaedic mattress is literally a thing somebody threw down.

cards.title: checkmate
cards.story: Shah mat is Persian for 'the king is helpless'. Chess came from India to Persia and then spread west. Arabic shah gave English check, and check gave us the word cheque and even the Exchequer, named after its checked cloth counting table.

cards.title: paradise
cards.hook: Its first meaning was a garden wall.
cards.story: Ancient Persian pairi-daeza meant an enclosed garden: pairi, around, daeza, wall. Persian royal parks so dazzled the Greeks that paradeisos became the word for heaven. The next time you feel fenced in, remember paradise is named after a wall.

cards.title: tulip
cards.hook: A flower named after a hat.
cards.story: The bloom was said to look like a Turkish turban, tülbent, so Europeans named the flower after the hat. A slip in the borrowing turned the word into tulip. The fortunes lost in the Dutch tulip craze of 1637 were, by name, lost on headgear.

cards.title: ketchup
cards.story: Ke-tsiap was a fermented fish sauce made by Chinese sailors and traders. The British brought it home and spent centuries trying to copy it, with walnuts, mushrooms, anything, until Americans added tomatoes. Today it is sweet, red and in denial.

cards.title: tycoon
cards.hook: A shogun's title in Silicon Valley.
cards.story: Taikun meant 'great lord' in Japanese, a title used for the shogun in dealings with foreigners. Commodore Perry's Americans brought it home in the 1850s. Within a few years, Abraham Lincoln's secretaries were calling him The Tycoon.

cards.title: emoji
cards.hook: It has nothing to do with emotion.
cards.story: E means picture and moji means character in Japanese. Emoji has no etymological link with 'emotion'. The resemblance is one of the happiest coincidences in the history of language, which is probably worth a smiley.

cards.title: karaoke
cards.story: Kara means empty and oke is short for okesutora, the Japanese borrowing of orchestra. So karaoke literally means 'empty orchestra'. The instrument is missing and the singing, as is widely known, is often missing too.

cards.title: tsunami
cards.story: Tsu means harbour and nami means wave. The story goes that Japanese fishermen, out at sea, felt nothing unusual, then came home to find their harbour wrecked. The name records exactly what it looked like from the shore.

cards.title: honcho
cards.story: Hancho means squad leader in Japanese, and American soldiers in Japan and Korea picked it up in the 1950s. Now a 'head honcho' runs your company, which, if you think about it, makes that person a head head.

cards.title: sky
cards.hook: The Vikings gave it to us.
cards.story: Old Norse sky meant a cloud. English had heofon for the whole overhead, and kept it for the religious sense, but the Viking word took over the rest. Standing under a blue English sky, you are technically looking at a cloud.

cards.title: window
cards.story: Vindauga, in Old Norse, joined vindr, wind, and auga, eye. A window was a hole in the wall that the wind looked through. English dropped its own 'eye-hole' and borrowed the Viking word. The poet in you should insist on wind eye.

cards.title: they
cards.story: English pronouns are almost never borrowed. Yet they, them and their are Viking: Old Norse their, replacing Old English hie. That shows how close the two peoples lived. You cannot get a word more everyday than 'they'.

cards.title: berserk
cards.story: A berserkr was a Viking warrior who fought in a frenzy. The name probably means 'bear shirt', from wearing bearskin, though some prefer 'bare shirt', meaning fighting without armour. Scholars still argue. Either way, going berserk is best done at a distance.

cards.title: ransack
cards.story: Rannsaka was a formal Norse legal term: a search of a house for stolen goods, with rann meaning house. In England it drifted from official search to violent plunder. Anyone who has watched a cat enter a bedroom will understand how.

cards.title: egg
cards.story: In 1490, William Caxton told of merchants stranded off Kent who asked a housewife for 'eggys'. She said she spoke no French. Someone then asked for 'eyren', the southern word, and she understood. The Norse word won. English nearly lost its breakfast.

cards.title: slogan
cards.story: A sluagh-ghairm was a Highland clan's battle cry, literally 'army shout'. English made it slogan in the 1500s. Modern adverts are still shouting, only now it is about cereal.

cards.title: whisky
cards.hook: The Gaelic for water of life.
cards.story: Uisge beatha means 'water of life' in Gaelic, and it shrank to whisky. Scandinavian aquavit also means water of life, as does French eau de vie. Russian vodka means just 'little water'. Everybody calls the strong stuff water.

cards.title: galore
cards.hook: A word that must stand after the noun.
cards.story: Irish go leor means 'enough' or 'plenty'. English added it after its nouns: 'whisky galore'. It is one of the very few English adjectives that always goes after the noun. Sometimes a word's best trick is where it sits.
cards.try: There were bargains galore at the book fair.

cards.title: pistol
cards.story: Czech Hussite rebels in the 1420s named a small handgun pistala, which means a pipe or flute, for its shape. The word spread through German and French and became pistol. Western movies owe a dramatic word to a Czech flute.

cards.title: boss
cards.story: American colonists took Dutch baas from New York, perhaps because they were reluctant to call anyone 'master', a word too close to slavery. Your entire corporate vocabulary may rest on someone avoiding a worse word.

cards.title: cookie
cards.hook: The Dutch baked your browser data.
cards.story: Dutch koekje means 'little cake', and Dutch settlers in New York passed it to American English. Then, in 1994, a web browser engineer named a small stored packet of data a cookie. Every 'accept cookies' pop-up is still speaking Dutch.

cards.title: easel
cards.story: Ezel is Dutch for donkey. Painters called the stand an ezel because it carried the weight, as a donkey would. The same joke runs through 'clothes horse'. Every easel in a Paris studio is, by name, a patient small donkey.

cards.title: yacht
cards.hook: The Dutch built them to chase.
cards.story: Jaghtschip meant 'ship for chasing'. The speedy Dutch boats caught the eye of Charles II during his exile, and he brought the idea to England. The spelling, inherited from the Dutch, has been defeating schoolchildren ever since.

cards.title: coleslaw
cards.hook: It has nothing to do with cold.
cards.story: Dutch koolsla is simply 'cabbage salad', kool meaning cabbage. English speakers assumed it must be 'cold slaw' and began spelling it so, for over a century, with a 'hot slaw' to match. Salads, apparently, do not like being misheard.

cards.title: chocolate
cards.hook: No one is sure of the word.
cards.story: Chocolate came to Spanish from Nahuatl, the Aztec language, but its exact parent is disputed. The popular derivation, xocolatl, 'bitter water', does not appear in early sources. The world's favourite sweet word has a mysterious, possibly invented, origin.

cards.title: avocado
cards.story: Aztec ahuacatl sounded to Spanish ears so much like abogado, a lawyer, that avocado was born. English has since added 'alligator pear' for good measure. The fruit on your toast is, in a small way, a Spanish legal mistake.

cards.title: hurricane
cards.story: Hurakan was a Taino word for the great storms of the Caribbean. Spanish sailors took it, and English spelt it dozens of ways before settling. Shakespeare wrote 'hurricano'. The Taino world was devastated by the Spanish, but its word is on every weather map.

cards.title: barbecue
cards.story: Barbacoa was a Taino raised wooden frame for cooking or sleeping on. Spanish explorers carried the word back, and it eventually came to mean the whole outdoor feast. Every Sunday barbecue honours a Caribbean wooden rack.

cards.title: cannibal
cards.story: Columbus recorded a people called the Caniba, his rendering of Carib. He claimed they ate human flesh, which conveniently justified enslaving them. Their name became our word for eating people. History has, for once, tracked the slander all the way back.

cards.title: kangaroo
cards.story: Cook's crew, the tale goes, pointed at the animal and asked its name, and 'kangaroo' meant 'I don't know'. It is a fable. Linguist John Haviland studied Guugu Yimithirr in the 1970s: gangurru is simply the word for a large grey kangaroo.

cards.title: taboo
cards.story: In 1777, Captain Cook recorded the Tongan word tabu for things forbidden. English had no word for a ban that was sacred and social at once. Now it means anything you should not say at dinner, which is a long way for a Tongan word to have travelled.

cards.title: tattoo
cards.story: English has two tattoos. The ink comes from Tahitian tatau, brought back by Cook's crew. The military drum display comes from Dutch taptoe, 'shut the tap', the signal for bars to stop serving. So the Edinburgh Tattoo is named after last orders.

cards.title: dollar
cards.hook: A Czech valley is in your wallet.
cards.story: Silver coins minted at Joachimsthal in Bohemia were called Joachimsthalers, then thalers, which English spelt dollar. A Czech valley named after St Joachim gave its name to the world's reserve currency. The American dollar is a Bohemian immigrant.

cards.title: cravat
cards.hook: A neck scarf fought a war.
cards.story: Croatian soldiers fighting for France in the 1600s wore striking knotted neck scarves. The French called the style a la croate, and cravate followed. Every necktie in every office is named after a Croatian soldier.

cards.title: denim
cards.story: Serge de Nimes, cloth from the French town of Nimes, shrank to denim. Jeans themselves are from Genoa, whose sailors' trousers the French called Genes. So one garment quietly names two cities. Neither is in America, whatever your jeans might tell you.

cards.title: turkey
cards.hook: No one knows where this bird is from.
cards.story: English named the American bird after Turkey. The Turks call it hindi, from India. The French say dinde, 'of India'. The Portuguese call it peru. Almost everyone on earth blamed somebody else's country for it.

cards.title: canary
cards.hook: The islands were named for dogs.
cards.story: The Canary Islands are not named after the birds. Roman writer Pliny says the islands had many dogs, so: Canaria insula, Isle of Dogs. The birds got their name from the islands. A small yellow bird is, etymologically, a dog.

cards.title: syrup
cards.story: Arabic shariba means 'to drink'. From it came sharbat, which is also where English sherbet started. Syrup comes from the same root, and so does shrub, a fruit cordial. Your sharbat and your pancake syrup are sipping from the same old Arabic well.

cards.title: coffee
cards.story: Qahwa, the Arabic word, may have first meant a kind of wine, before being applied to the dark drink from roasted beans. Turks made it kahve and Italians caffe. The word's first meaning is still being argued over, ideally with coffee in hand.

cards.title: mortgage
cards.story: Old French mort gage means 'dead pledge'. The deal dies when the debt is paid, or the property is lost to you if it is not. Either way, something dies. Anyone who has paid one for twenty years knows this was not a metaphor.

cards.title: guerrilla
cards.story: Spanish guerra means war, so guerrilla means 'little war', coined when Spanish irregulars harried Napoleon's troops after 1808. Fighters later took the name. The term 'guerrilla marketing' is a small war for your attention.

cards.title: average
cards.story: When merchants' goods were damaged at sea, they shared the loss equally. Italian avaria, probably from Arabic awar, 'damage', named this fair split. English average grew from it. Your CAT percentile rests on shipwreck accounting.

cards.title: monsoon
cards.story: Arab sailors timed their Indian Ocean crossings by the wind, and called it mawsim, the season. The Portuguese made it moncao, and English monsoon. To India the word means everything. To the Arab navigator it was simply the time to set sail.

cards.title: typhoon
cards.story: Typhoon may come from Greek Typhon, a monster; from Arabic tufan, a flood; or from Chinese tai fung, great wind. All these similar words have blended, and no one can untangle them fully. Language has its storms too.

cards.title: mayday
cards.hook: Not about a day in May.
cards.story: The radio distress call comes from French m'aidez or m'aider, 'help me'. The story goes that a Croydon radio officer picked it in the early 1920s, because so much traffic flew to Paris. Whoever chose it, one word can now summon the world.

cards.title: penguin
cards.hook: The name does not match the bird.
cards.story: Penguin may come from Welsh pen gwyn, 'white head', a name sailors first gave the great auk of the North Atlantic. Penguins have black heads, and scholars dispute the Welsh. The great auk, which did fit the name, went extinct in 1844.

cards.title: boondocks
cards.hook: A mountain became the back of beyond.
cards.story: Bundok means mountain in Tagalog. US soldiers in the Philippines around 1900 picked up the word and brought it back as 'the boondocks': the back of beyond. Now it means nowhere much, all because some Filipinos pointed at a mountain.

cards.title: amok
cards.hook: It once meant a desperate charge.
cards.story: Malay amuk was a desperate, frenzied fighting charge. Portuguese and English visitors described men 'running amok', and the phrase is now so domestic that we use it for toddlers and office printers.

cards.title: tea
cards.hook: How did it reach your kitchen?
cards.story: Almost every language on earth calls it either te or cha, and the difference is a map of trade. Cha travelled by land through Persia and became chai. Te went by sea with the Dutch, from Hokkien ports. When you order 'chai tea', you are saying both.

cards.title: salary
cards.hook: Roman soldiers were not paid in salt.
cards.story: You may have heard that Roman soldiers were paid in salt. There is no good evidence for it. Latin salarium does come from sal, salt, and may have been an allowance connected with salt. But the neat story of wages paid in salt is a modern embellishment.

cards.title: bankrupt
cards.hook: A bench broken in the market.
cards.story: Italian money-dealers worked at a bench, the banca, which gave us bank. A failed dealer was banca rotta, 'broken bench', and the word reached English as bankrupt. Whether the bench was really smashed in public is disputed, but the image has outlived the bench.

cards.title: ghost
cards.hook: The h is a ghost too.
cards.story: Old English gast had no h. Then William Caxton's print shop, staffed by men used to Flemish gheest, added one in the 1480s. The fashion spread to ghastly too. The h in ghost is itself a ghost: a letter with no body and no sound.

cards.title: debt
cards.story: Medieval English spelt it dette, as the French did, and nobody said a b, because there was no b. Renaissance scholars, showing off their Latin, added one to match debitum. We have been paying interest on that b ever since.

cards.title: doubt
cards.story: Chaucer wrote 'doute'. Then Renaissance scholars, anxious to show the word came from Latin dubitare, pushed in a b. Nobody pronounced it. Nobody ever has. Five hundred years later, every schoolchild still has to spell a letter put there for show.

cards.title: island
cards.story: Island comes from Old English igland, with no s at all. Scholars assumed it must be related to French isle and Latin insula, so they added one. It is unrelated. The s in island is an error in a word for dry land, surrounded by a sea of bad guesses.

cards.title: scissors
cards.hook: A Latin mix-up added the c.
cards.story: Middle English had sisoures, from Latin cisorium, a cutting tool. Someone wrongly linked it to Latin scindere, to split, and added an sc. Nobody says the c. A pair of scissors is really a pair of spelling mistakes joined at a hinge.

cards.title: receipt
cards.story: A Latin-loving fashion stuck a p into receipt, after recepta. The p was never said. Conceit and deceit escaped the treatment and stayed p-free. So English ended up with an extra letter on every bill you have ever paid.

cards.title: salmon
cards.hook: A silent l, by order of Rome.
cards.story: English borrowed saumon from French with no l. Scholars then inserted one to honour Latin salmo. Almost nobody started pronouncing it. Fortunately, few people have to spell it, and those who do are usually more concerned about the bones.

cards.title: victuals
cards.hook: The old spelling is still how it sounds.
cards.story: The word for food was vitaille in Old French and vittles in English. A Latin-minded spelling forced in a c, after victualia, and the result looks like a trap. It is still said 'vittles'. The spelling never did manage to teach the mouth.

cards.title: indict
cards.hook: Say it wrong and learn something.
cards.story: Medieval English spelt it indite, matching the sound. Renaissance scholars stuck in a c to show off the Latin indictare. The spelling changed, the sound did not. To this day you indict someone by saying 'indite', and the letter c stands mute in court.

cards.title: could
cards.hook: An l added by peer pressure.
cards.story: Could had no l. Its neighbours would and should really did have one, once. In the early 1500s an l was added to could, just to match. The word that means ability was given a useless letter out of sheer neighbourly envy.

cards.title: delight
cards.hook: It was never related to light.
cards.story: Delight comes from Old French delit, pleasure, with no g and no h. English writers saw 'light' and assumed a family link, so they restyled the spelling. Delight and light are not relations. They just stood next to each other long enough to look alike.

cards.title: ptarmigan
cards.hook: The p is a Greek pretence.
cards.story: A plain Scottish bird called the tarmachan had no p. Then someone assumed it must be Greek, like pterodactyl, from the Greek for wing, and added one. The bird is Gaelic through and through. Greek has never once come into it.

cards.title: colonel
cards.story: Italian colonnello came to French, which changed the first l to r: coronel. English borrowed coronel and said it with an r. Then scholars changed the spelling back to an l. The spelling went Italian, the sound stayed French, and nobody told the mouth.

cards.title: rhyme
cards.story: Rime is the honest spelling. English scholars, noticing rhythm, decided rime ought to match, and stuck in an h. Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner is spelt correctly. Every rhyme you have ever written is wearing a borrowed letter.

cards.title: aisle
cards.story: An aisle was an 'ele', a wing, from Latin ala. English got it muddled with isle, which gave it an s, then matched French aile, which gave it an a. Now all those letters spell a sound that could be written with one: I.

cards.title: sovereign
cards.hook: A king with a stolen g.
cards.story: French soverain had no g at all. English writers assumed it must be related to reign, and added one. It is not related to reign, or to the g. Foreign was treated the same way. Royal spelling, in English, is largely a matter of imagination.

cards.title: fault
cards.hook: The letter that changed the speech.
cards.story: Chaucer's 'faute' had no l. Scholars added one for Latin credentials, and for centuries nobody said it. Then people began reading the word as it looked, and the l came to life. Spelling, in this one odd case, changed how English sounds.

cards.title: Ye Olde
cards.story: Medieval English had a letter, thorn, þ, for the sound th. Early printers using continental type had no thorn, so they used y instead. So 'ye olde shoppe' was always read as 'the old shop'. The Ye in every tourist teashop is a typographical fossil.

cards.title: dord
cards.hook: A dictionary invented a word by accident.
cards.story: A 1934 Webster's dictionary defined dord as density. The word did not exist. An editor's note, 'D or d', meant density could be abbreviated, and the letters were run together. For years dord sat in print, a ghost word haunting a dictionary.

cards.title: The Great Vowel Shift
cards.story: Between about 1400 and 1700, the long vowels of English drifted upward in the mouth, in a slow chain reaction nobody can fully explain. 'Mouse' used to sound like 'moose'. Spelling had just frozen, so you now read words written in a dead accent.

cards.title: knight
cards.story: In Old English every letter of cniht was pronounced: k, n, i and a throaty gh, like the ch in loch. The k and the gh later fell silent, but the spelling stayed. Knights, then, are words in armour, every silent letter an old soldier.

cards.title: one
cards.hook: A rogue w that should not be there.
cards.story: Old English an was said 'ahn'. Regional speech added a w at the front, and that sound won, although the spelling did not change. Only and alone kept the old vowel. Say 'alone' aloud and you are saying the old way of saying 'one'.

cards.title: Wednesday
cards.hook: A god is hiding in the calendar.
cards.story: Wednesday is Woden's day, and Thursday is Thor's. The d in Wednesday survives only in spelling, a ghost of the god's name that most speakers do not pronounce. Odin, the one-eyed Norse god of war and wisdom, sits quietly in your diary every week.

cards.title: ghoti
cards.hook: The famous joke is not Shaw's.
cards.story: Ghoti spells fish: gh from enough, o from women, ti from nation. People credit George Bernard Shaw, but it is not in his writings, and a letter of 1855 shows the joke is older. It is also cheating: gh is never f at the start of a word.

cards.title: Shakespeare
cards.hook: He never spelt it our way.
cards.story: Only six signatures by Shakespeare survive, and they vary: Shakp, Shaksper, Shakspere, Shakspeare. Not one is spelt the way we spell it. English spelling did not really exist yet, so not even its greatest writer could be wrong.

cards.title: The Long S
cards.hook: Those old fs are not fs.
cards.story: Old books seem to lisp: 'Congrefs', 'bleffed'. That is the long s, ſ, an old letter that looks almost like f. The Times dropped it in 1803 and printers everywhere followed. Every 18th-century f you laugh at was really an s in a hurry.

cards.title: The Letter J
cards.hook: It came late to the alphabet.
cards.story: J is one of the youngest letters. For centuries it was just a fancy form of i, and the first King James Bible of 1611 has no separate J at all: Jesus was Iesus. The letter only won full independence after that Bible went to press.

cards.title: upper case
cards.hook: It was literally the upper case.
cards.story: Printers kept capital letters in an upper wooden case and small letters in a lower one, within arm's reach. That is the whole origin of upper case and lower case. The everyday terms on your phone keyboard describe how a workshop was organised.

cards.title: W
cards.hook: The letter is misnamed, sort of.
cards.story: W is called 'double u' because Norman scribes really did write it as two u's. Later, u and v became separate letters, and the printed form looks like two v's. So a w looks like two v's and is named after two u's. English could not settle on one letter.

cards.title: color
cards.story: Noah Webster's 1806 dictionary cut the u from colour and the k from musick, and Americans followed him. He also tried tung and wimmen, which failed completely. Every time a spellcheck insults you, a long-dead American lexicographer is involved.

cards.title: -ough
cards.story: Though, through, rough, cough, bough, thought, thorough: the same four letters, many sounds. The gh was once a throaty sound, which then changed or vanished differently in each word while the spelling stood still. Spelling is a photograph of dead speech.

cards.title: hiccough
cards.hook: There is no cough in it.
cards.story: Hiccup is the honest spelling, after the sound itself. Then someone decided it must be connected to cough and wrote hiccough, and the misspelling has been politely sitting in dictionaries ever since. Say it out loud: there is no cough in it.

cards.title: apron
cards.hook: The n went for a walk.
cards.story: A cook once wore a napron. Said quickly, 'a napron' and 'an apron' sound identical, and over time the n slid across the gap. The same family of words gave us napkin, which kept its n, and apron, which lost it.

cards.title: adder
cards.hook: A snake that lost a letter.
cards.story: Old English had nædre for a snake, and German still has Natter. Then 'a nadder' became 'an adder', the way a napron became an apron. Ordinary slack speech quietly took the n off the snake.

cards.title: umpire
cards.story: A noumpere was a 'non-peer', the neutral third person called in when two sides could not agree. A noumpere became an umpire. So the word that decides whether you are out was itself out by one letter, and never got a review.

cards.title: newt
