cards.hook: The n went the other way.
cards.story: It was once an ewt. 'An ewt' ran together until it became 'a newt', the reverse of what happened to apron. Shakespeare's witches stir in an 'eye of newt', a recipe that would have looked quite different if the n had wandered back.

cards.title: nickname
cards.hook: You were given an extra name.
cards.story: Eke meant also, so an eke-name was an extra name. 'An eke-name' became 'a nickname' by the same slipping n that gave us a newt. So the affectionate names your friends have for you began as a mishearing.

cards.title: cherry
cards.hook: One cherry was mistaken for many.
cards.story: English borrowed cherise from Old North French. Hearing that final s, English speakers assumed it was a plural and took off the ending. English did the same with pease, giving us a pea. Every single pea is a grammar error.

cards.title: sherry
cards.hook: The bottle was mistaken for many.
cards.story: Sherry is named after Jerez in Spain, which English drinkers wrote as sherris. Sherris sounded plural, so they dropped the s and ordered a sherry. Shakespeare's Falstaff praised 'sherris-sack'. One Spanish town became one English singular by accident.

cards.title: alligator
cards.story: Spanish el lagarto means 'the lizard'. English sailors in the Americas heard it as one word and called the creature an alligator. We then went on to add our own 'the'. So the alligator is, in a sense, 'the the lizard'.

cards.title: cockroach
cards.story: Cucaracha looked too foreign, so English speakers turned it into two familiar words, cock and roach, neither of which describes the insect. A cock is a rooster, and a roach is a fish. It remains the least accurate name in your kitchen.

cards.title: crayfish
cards.hook: It is not a fish at all.
cards.story: Old French crevice meant a crab or crayfish. English heard the end as 'fish', which seemed reasonable for something in a river, and rebuilt the word around it. A crayfish is no fish. It is a small mistake with claws.

cards.title: bridegroom
cards.story: Brydguma, in Old English, meant 'bride's man', guma being an old word for man. When guma died out, confused speakers swapped in the word groom, which meant a lad and, later, a horse-servant. Every groom at every wedding is a linguistic accident.

cards.title: sirloin
cards.hook: No king ever knighted a cut of beef.
cards.story: A much-loved tale says an English king enjoyed his beef so much that he knighted it 'Sir Loin'. Several kings get the credit, which should make you suspicious. The word is French surlonge, the part above the loin. No beef has ever been knighted.

cards.title: humble pie
cards.story: Numbles were a deer's heart and liver, the cheap parts kept for servants. A numble pie became an umble pie, and then a humble pie, pulled toward the word humble. To eat humble pie was literally to eat the offal, while your betters had the roast.

cards.title: forlorn hope
cards.hook: There is no hope in it at all.
cards.story: Verloren hoop is Dutch for 'lost troop', the soldiers sent first into a breach, knowing most would die. English heard 'forlorn hope' and imagined a sad wish. The original meant a doomed squad, and the misreading is more hopeful than the truth.

cards.title: penthouse
cards.hook: The luxury flat is a shed.
cards.story: Apentis was a lean-to shed stuck against a bigger building. In English it became pentis, then, by a slip of the ear, penthouse. So the most expensive apartment in any city is named after a shed.

cards.title: belfry
cards.hook: It had nothing to do with bells.
cards.story: A berfrey was a movable siege tower pushed up against castle walls. Towers also held bells, so English ears heard bell, and the word became belfry. The bell was an afterthought. Bats in the belfry are living in what was once a siege weapon.

cards.title: tawdry
cards.story: St Audrey of Ely died, it is said, of a throat tumour she saw as punishment for her youthful necklaces. A fair in her name sold cheap lace neckwear, 'St Audrey's lace'. 'Seynt Audrey' slurred into tawdry. A saint's regret became a word for trashy.

cards.title: ampersand
cards.hook: A letter that fell off the alphabet.
cards.story: Schoolchildren once recited the alphabet with & at the end, saying 'and per se and', meaning '& by itself is and'. Slurred through thousands of classrooms, that phrase became ampersand. A symbol's name was created purely by chanting.

cards.title: zenith
cards.story: Arabic samt ar-ras means 'path over the head'. A medieval scribe copying it into Latin misread m as ni, producing senit, which became zenith. So the word for the very highest point began with a slip at a copyist's desk.

cards.title: scapegoat
cards.story: Translating Leviticus in 1530, William Tyndale met Hebrew azazel, which many scholars now take as a name, and read it as ez ozel, 'the goat that departs'. He wrote 'scape goat', the goat that escapes. Someone's guess has been carrying the blame ever since.

cards.title: female
cards.hook: It has no connection to male.
cards.story: Female does not come from male. It comes from Old French femelle, a small woman, and was only reshaped in English to rhyme with male. The words look like a pair. They are, historically, strangers who have been standing together for several hundred years.

cards.title: asparagus
cards.hook: Birds had nothing to do with it.
cards.story: For two centuries, English speakers called asparagus 'sparrow-grass', since that at least made some sense. The Greek word had no sparrows in it and no grass. Dictionaries disapproved, and the sparrows slowly flew away, but they took their time.

cards.title: rosemary
cards.hook: No roses, no Mary, just sea.
cards.story: Latin ros marinus means 'dew of the sea', because the plant grows near the coast. English speakers heard 'rose' and 'Mary', which sounded religious and lovely, and reshaped the word. No rose and no Mary were ever involved.

cards.title: helpmeet
cards.story: Genesis calls Eve 'an help meet for him', meaning a suitable helper. Readers ran the two words together into helpmeet, and then turned it into helpmate. An adjective in the Bible became a noun for a spouse, and the word 'meet', meaning fit, has gone.

cards.title: shamefaced
cards.hook: It was never about the face.
cards.story: Shamefast meant fixed in modesty, just as steadfast means fixed in place. English speakers misheard it as shamefaced, which sounded sensible, and a face appeared where there had never been one. Steadfast, luckily, stayed steadfast.

cards.title: hamburger
cards.hook: There is no ham in it.
cards.story: Hamburger steak was named after the German port of Hamburg. English speakers assumed the ham was in the first half and started inventing burgers: cheeseburger, beefburger. A bit of German geography has since been chopped into a suffix.

cards.title: helicopter
cards.hook: You have been splitting this wrong.
cards.story: Helicopter joins Greek helix, spiral, and pteron, wing, as in pterodactyl. So the true split is helico-pter. Everyone instead heard heli plus copter, which gave us heliport and helipad. A word part that never existed now lands on hospital roofs.

cards.title: burgle
cards.story: Burglar is centuries old. Its verb, burgle, appeared in the late 1860s as a joke, taking the -ar off as if a burglar were someone who burgles. It was thought comic, and many dictionaries sniffed at it. The jokers won. You can be burgled in any modern court.

cards.title: asset
cards.hook: One asset was never meant to exist.
cards.story: Assets comes from Anglo-French asetz, 'enough', meaning enough to pay your debts. It was a singular that sounded plural. Someone invented 'an asset', which makes no sense grammatically and has since been worth billions.

cards.title: bus
cards.story: A French transport company in the 1820s named its service the omnibus, Latin for 'for all'. English chopped off omni, keeping bus, which was only the grammatical ending. You are riding a Latin case ending to work.

cards.title: mob
cards.hook: The slang that annoyed Jonathan Swift.
cards.story: Mobile vulgus, Latin for 'fickle crowd', was clipped in 17th-century slang to the mobile, then to mob. Jonathan Swift publicly hated this lazy new word. It stayed, as the crowd generally does.

cards.title: sabotage
cards.hook: The clog story has a flaw.
cards.story: Workers hurling wooden clogs, sabots, into machines is a wonderful tale. But French saboter already meant to clatter about or bungle a job before any such revolt is recorded. The word probably came from clumsy feet, not from thrown shoes.

cards.title: posh
cards.hook: 'Port out, starboard home' is a fib.
cards.story: The story says wealthy passengers to India booked Port Out, Starboard Home for the cooler side, and POSH was stamped on tickets. P&O has no such record, and no such ticket has ever surfaced. The word's real origin is still unknown.

cards.title: golf
cards.story: 'Gentlemen Only, Ladies Forbidden' is a joke, not an etymology. The word golf is centuries older than acronyms and comes from Scots gouf, usually traced to Dutch kolf, a club. The acronym story was invented much later, quite possibly on a golf course.

cards.title: sincere
cards.story: Sculptors hid cracks with wax, we are told, so sincere means sine cera, 'without wax'. There is no ancient evidence for this, and the Oxford English Dictionary finds no probability in it. A lovely story and, like most lovely word stories, not true at all.

cards.title: rule of thumb
cards.story: Claims that English law let men beat their wives with a stick no thicker than a thumb have no legal basis. The phrase appears in print from 1685 with no such meaning, and scholars traced the myth to the 1970s. It means simply a rough measure by hand.

cards.title: crap
cards.story: Thomas Crapper was a real Victorian plumber, but he did not invent the flush toilet and he did not give us the word crap, which was around long before him. The universe's greatest coincidence of surname and occupation is merely that.

cards.title: SOS
cards.story: SOS does not mean Save Our Souls or Save Our Ship. It was adopted by international convention in 1906 simply because three dots, three dashes and three dots are impossible to miss. The words were made up afterwards to fit the letters.

cards.title: quiz
cards.hook: A very good story, and very unlikely.
cards.story: Dublin theatre manager Richard Daly supposedly bet in 1791 that he could make a made-up word famous overnight, and chalked 'quiz' on walls. But the tale first appears in 1835, and the word was already in print by the 1780s. Nobody knows its true origin.

cards.title: Ring a Ring o' Roses
cards.story: The rosy rash, the sneezing, the falling down: surely this is the Great Plague? Folklorists say no. The rhyme was not printed until 1881, and the plague reading appears only in the 20th century. A dark story, invented by adults, about a children's game.

cards.title: serendipity
cards.hook: A fairy tale about Sri Lanka did it.
cards.story: Horace Walpole, in a letter of 1754, described a fairy tale, The Three Princes of Serendip, whose heroes keep discovering things they were not looking for. Serendip is an old name for Sri Lanka. So English's word for happy accidents is named after an island.

cards.title: robot
cards.hook: A Czech word for forced labour.
cards.story: Karel Čapek needed a word for artificial workers in his 1920 play R.U.R. His brother Josef suggested robota, the Czech for forced labour. The play ends badly for humanity, as such stories tend to. Every robot since is named after a drudge.

cards.title: pandemonium
cards.story: In Paradise Lost, Milton needed a name for the capital of Hell and built Pandemonium: pan, all, and daimon, demon. Milton meant it grandly. English took one look at the place and decided it meant a noisy mess.

cards.title: chortle
cards.hook: A word built from two noises.
cards.story: 'He chortled in his joy', wrote Lewis Carroll in Through the Looking-Glass. He had mashed chuckle and snort together and, unusually, the joke stuck. Humpty Dumpty calls such words portmanteaus, a use Carroll also invented.

cards.title: nerd
cards.hook: A children's book may have birthed it.
cards.story: In If I Ran the Zoo (1950), Dr Seuss lists 'a Nerkle, a Nerd, and a Seersucker too'. A year later, nerd turns up as American slang for a square. No one can prove the link, but the word now runs Silicon Valley. The Seersucker, alas, faded.

cards.title: quark
cards.hook: Physics, from a line of nonsense.
cards.story: Murray Gell-Mann named a new family of subatomic particles quarks, after a line in James Joyce's Finnegans Wake: 'Three quarks for Muster Mark'. The line was nonsense. It then turned out that every proton is made of exactly three.

cards.title: gas
cards.story: In the 1600s, Flemish chemist Jan van Helmont needed a word for what came off burning charcoal. Inspired by Greek khaos, he wrote gas, the g said the Flemish way. Your LPG cylinder is, by etymology, a tank of chaos.

cards.title: blurb
cards.hook: Miss Belinda Blurb is to blame.
cards.story: At a booksellers' dinner in 1907, humorist Gelett Burgess handed out a book jacket featuring a gushing young woman called Miss Belinda Blurb, shouting its praises. The joke worked so well that every back cover since has had a blurb.

cards.title: yahoo
cards.hook: Founders named a firm after brutes.
cards.story: Yahoos are the filthy, brutal humans of Gulliver's Travels (1726), kept by civilised horses. Jonathan Swift made up the word. Two Stanford students, aware of the joke, named their internet directory after them in the 1990s.

cards.title: utopia
cards.hook: A place that cannot exist, by name.
cards.story: Sir Thomas More coined Utopia in 1516 for a perfect imaginary island. The name is a pun: Greek ou-topos, no place, sounds like eu-topos, good place. The perfect society was, in its very title, quietly declared impossible.

cards.title: catch-22
cards.story: Joseph Heller's war novel was going to be called Catch-18, until Leon Uris's Mila 18 got there first. So he changed the number. The double bind that bears his book's name was, ironically, caught in a bind of its own.

cards.title: googol
cards.story: Mathematician Edward Kasner asked his nephew Milton, nine, to name a 1 followed by 100 zeros. Milton said 'googol'. Decades later, two Stanford students misspelt it for their search engine. The internet's biggest name began as a child's guess.

cards.title: scientist
cards.story: Before 1833, people who studied nature were 'natural philosophers'. At a British Association meeting, William Whewell, challenged to find a name, suggested 'scientist', by analogy with artist. So Newton and Galileo were never called scientists in their lives.

cards.title: dinosaur
cards.story: In 1842, Richard Owen coined Dinosauria from Greek deinos, terrible, and sauros, lizard. The word stuck, though scientists later found dinosaurs are not lizards at all. Birds, apparently, are dinosaurs. You could call a pigeon a terrible lizard.

cards.title: agnostic
cards.hook: The man who said 'I do not know'.
cards.story: Biologist T. H. Huxley needed a word for his position in 1869: that the existence of God could not be known. He built agnostic from Greek a-, not, and gnostos, known. A word for honest uncertainty was, oddly, invented on purpose.

cards.title: meme
cards.hook: Long before the internet had any.
cards.story: In The Selfish Gene (1976), Richard Dawkins needed a word for an idea that spreads like a gene, and shortened Greek mimema, something imitated, to rhyme with gene. He meant tunes and fashions. The cat pictures came later.

cards.title: Kodak
cards.hook: A word built for a trademark.
cards.story: George Eastman liked the letter K, a strong and incisive letter, he said. He played with combinations until he had Kodak, which meant nothing in any language. It was short, hard to misspell, and needed no translation. Brands have chased it ever since.

cards.title: factoid
cards.hook: The word is itself a factoid.
cards.story: Norman Mailer coined factoid in 1973 for something that looks like a fact but isn't, using -oid as in humanoid. English then took it to mean 'a small fact'. So the common use of factoid is itself a factoid.

cards.title: Big Bang
cards.hook: The theory's name came from its critic.
cards.story: Astronomer Fred Hoyle, who did not believe the universe had a beginning, called the idea 'this big bang' on BBC radio in 1949. He later denied he meant to mock it. Either way, the name given by its greatest critic is now the theory's official name.

cards.title: Impressionism
cards.hook: A critic meant it as an insult.
cards.story: In 1874, art critic Louis Leroy saw Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise and sneered that the painters were mere 'impressionists'. The insult was so good the painters took it on. Some of the world's most expensive paintings bear the name of a sneer.

cards.title: gobbledygook
cards.story: Maury Maverick, a former Texas congressman, fought government jargon in 1944 with a new word, gobbledygook, perhaps from turkeys gobbling in the yard. He was the grandson of Samuel Maverick, the rancher who gave us maverick. Two words from one family.

cards.title: scofflaw
cards.hook: A word made to order, for money.
cards.story: In 1923, a Prohibition campaigner offered $200 for a new word for someone who drinks illegally. Out of more than twenty thousand entries, scofflaw won in January 1924. It outlived Prohibition, and now describes people who ignore parking tickets.

cards.title: mondegreen
cards.story: Writer Sylvia Wright grew up hearing a Scottish ballad as 'They hae slain the Earl o' Moray, and Lady Mondegreen.' The real words: 'and laid him on the green.' In 1954 she named all such misheard lyrics mondegreens, after the lady who was never there.

cards.title: eggcorn
cards.story: Someone wrote 'egg corn' for acorn, a mistake that actually makes sense: it is egg-shaped and like a grain. In 2003, linguist Geoffrey Pullum proposed eggcorn as the name for such sensible errors, as in 'for all intensive purposes'.

cards.title: vitamin
cards.hook: It lost its e, and for good reason.
cards.story: In 1912, Casimir Funk called his discovery a 'vitamine', a vital amine. When scientists found many vitamins are not amines at all, they simply dropped the e. You are taking, on its own label, a correction to a chemistry error.

cards.title: oxygen
cards.story: Lavoisier named oxygen from Greek oxys, sharp or acid, and -gen, producer, because he believed it made all acids. He was wrong. Acids, it turned out, depend on hydrogen. We have been breathing a chemist's error ever since.

cards.title: vaccine
cards.story: Vaccine comes from Latin vacca, a cow. In 1796, Edward Jenner protected a boy from smallpox using cowpox. Louis Pasteur later extended the word to all such treatments in Jenner's honour. So every vaccine, including the Covid jab, is named after a cow.

cards.title: electricity
cards.story: William Gilbert wrote in 1600 of the force that makes rubbed amber attract straw, using Latin electricus, from Greek elektron, amber. Sir Thomas Browne gave us 'electricity' in 1646. Every time you charge your phone, you are flattering fossilised tree sap.

cards.title: cyberspace
cards.hook: A word that predates the web.
cards.story: Cyberspace was coined by William Gibson in a 1982 story, when he had barely used a computer. He typed his novel Neuromancer on a typewriter. The man who named the internet's landscape imagined it using a machine that had no screen.

cards.title: malapropism
cards.story: Mrs Malaprop, in Sheridan's 1775 play The Rivals, always grabbed the wrong long word: 'as headstrong as an allegory on the banks of the Nile'. Her name, from French mal a propos, 'inappropriately', became the word for this special kind of blunder.

cards.title: satyagraha
cards.hook: A newspaper contest helped coin it.
cards.story: In South Africa, Gandhi offered a small newspaper prize for a better name than 'passive resistance'. His young relative Maganlal suggested sadagraha, firmness in a good cause. Gandhi altered it to satyagraha, 'holding firmly to truth', and it changed history.

cards.title: Tollywood
cards.story: An American engineer in Calcutta, Wilford Deming, joked in 1932 about Tollygunge's film studios and landed on Tollywood. Decades later, Bombay's industry borrowed the pattern. Bollywood is, strictly, a copy of a Calcutta joke, from a Hollywood original.

cards.title: hello
cards.story: When the telephone arrived, Alexander Graham Bell wanted everyone to answer with 'ahoy'. In an 1877 letter, Thomas Edison recommended 'hello!'. Edison's word won. The polite greeting of the whole world is a victory in a minor technical dispute.

cards.title: OK
cards.hook: The most successful joke ever told.
cards.story: In 1839, Boston papers enjoyed a craze for joke abbreviations. One was O.K., for 'oll korrect', a deliberate misspelling. Martin Van Buren's 1840 campaign then spread it as 'Old Kinderhook'. A joke spelling became one of the most understood words on earth.

cards.title: Shakespeare's Words
cards.hook: He did not invent nearly as many.
cards.story: Shakespeare is credited with inventing thousands of words, but the OED's early editors searched his works far more closely than anyone else's. Now that old books are digitised, many 'first uses' have moved earlier. He was a genius of use, not of invention.

cards.title: green-eyed monster
cards.story: In Othello, Iago warns that jealousy is 'the green-ey'd monster which doth mock the meat it feeds on'. Shakespeare gave us that image. Iago himself is the one feeding the monster, which is as good a reason as any not to trust a colleague's warnings.

cards.title: bug
cards.hook: The moth story is half true.
cards.story: Engineers on Harvard's Mark II found a moth in a relay in 1947 and taped it into the log: 'First actual case of bug being found.' Note the joke: engineers already said bugs. Thomas Edison was using the word for technical faults in 1878.

cards.title: cleave
cards.story: You can cleave a log in two, and a faithful spouse can cleave unto their partner. These are two separate Old English verbs, cleofan and clifian, which happened to crash into one spelling. A word that is its own opposite is called a contronym.

cards.title: sanction
cards.story: A government can sanction a plan, meaning allow it, or sanction a country, meaning punish it. Latin sanctio was a binding decree, which could carry reward or penalty. In a reading passage, one wrong guess about which one turns the answer upside down.
cards.try: The board sanctioned the merger; the regulator then sanctioned the board.

cards.title: oversight
cards.hook: Watching closely, or not at all.
cards.story: Oversight can mean careful supervision or a careless failure to notice. A government 'oversight committee' might commit an 'oversight', which would be perfectly grammatical and deeply ironic. Few words can have a fight inside a single sentence.

cards.title: fast
cards.story: Fast once meant firm, fixed: hold fast, stuck fast. Then someone 'ran fast', meaning with firmness and vigour, and the idea of speed took over. So a fast colour will not run, while a fast runner certainly does.

cards.title: The Old Man the Boat
cards.story: Try it: 'The old man the boat.' It seems to lack a verb, until you realise old is a noun and man is the verb: the elderly are staffing the boat. Your brain took the wrong path and had to walk back. Linguists call this a garden-path sentence.

cards.title: The Horse Raced Past the Barn Fell
cards.story: Linguist Thomas Bever used this sentence in 1970: 'The horse raced past the barn fell.' It is perfectly grammatical: the horse that was raced past the barn fell down. Most readers stall at 'fell'. It shows that we predict sentences as we read.

cards.title: The Buffalo Sentence
cards.story: 'Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo.' It is correct: bison from Buffalo, New York, whom other Buffalo bison bully, themselves bully Buffalo bison. Linguists have been building versions of this wonder since the 1960s.

cards.title: Time Flies Like an Arrow
cards.story: 'Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana.' The joke is often credited to Groucho Marx, without proof. The second half forces you to reread: flies is now a noun and like a verb. Computers trying to read English still find this kind of thing hard.

cards.title: The Quick Brown Fox
cards.story: 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' uses every letter of the alphabet. It was already a popular copybook line for pupils by 1885, and later went into typing manuals. In 1963 a version became the first message on the Moscow to Washington hotline.

cards.title: Mr Jock, TV Quiz PhD
cards.story: 'Mr Jock, TV quiz PhD, bags few lynx.' Twenty-six letters, each used just once. It is called a perfect pangram, and it reads like a tiny crime report. Writers go to great lengths to make these sound like English, and this is among their best.

cards.title: A Man, a Plan, a Canal: Panama
cards.story: Leigh Mercer published this palindrome in a 1948 issue of Notes and Queries: 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama'. Read it backwards, letter by letter. It is also a rather neat seven-word history of the Panama Canal.

cards.title: tattarrattat
cards.hook: The sound of a knock at the door.
cards.story: James Joyce invented tattarrattat in Ulysses for a knock on the door, and it reads the same in both directions, as a knock might. At twelve letters it is often cited as the longest palindrome in the Oxford English Dictionary.

cards.title: run
cards.hook: The hardest working word in English.
cards.story: Set was for a long time English's most versatile word. Then in 2011 the OED's Peter Gilliver reported that the verb run has 645 distinct meanings. You run a shop, run a fever, run out, run late. Language, it seems, never stands still.

cards.title: bookkeeper
cards.story: Bookkeeper has three double letters in a row: oo, kk, ee. It is one of the very few English words that can do that, and the accounting profession, not famous for flair, has never once thanked it.

cards.title: queue
cards.story: Queue starts with a q, and the four letters after it change nothing: remove them and the sound is the same. The word means 'tail' in French, and it is the perfect word for something English people do extremely well.

cards.title: facetious
cards.story: Facetious contains all five vowels in perfect alphabetical order: a, e, i, o, u. So does abstemious. Both are unusually well-behaved for English. It is a lovely fact, and a shame that only people being facetious ever mention it.

cards.title: typewriter
cards.story: Type 'typewriter' and you will use only the top row of a QWERTY keyboard. It is one of the longest common words that can be typed that way. There is a persistent legend that salesmen loved showing this off. It would be a very good trick if true.

cards.title: stewardesses
cards.story: Stewardesses, at twelve letters, can be typed with the left hand alone, one of the longest common words that can. Reverberated is another. If you ever want to give your right hand a rest, you know what to type.

cards.title: uncopyrightable
cards.story: Uncopyrightable has fifteen letters and uses none of them twice, which makes it an isogram. Dermatoglyphics, the study of skin patterns, is another. Whether uncopyrightable can itself be copyrighted is a question for your lawyer.

cards.title: sesquipedalian
cards.origin: Latin, 'a foot and a half long'
cards.story: The Roman poet Horace mocked long words as sesquipedalia verba, 'words a foot and a half long'. English duly made sesquipedalian, an adjective describing long words that is itself quite long. You cannot use it without committing the crime.

cards.title: pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis
cards.story: At forty-five letters it is the longest word in several major dictionaries, and its origin is a joke. Everett Smith of the National Puzzlers' League made it up in 1935 to be impressively long. It means a lung disease caused by inhaling very fine silica dust.

cards.title: floccinaucinihilipilification
cards.story: Floccinaucinihilipilification means judging something as worthless. It strings together four Latin words for 'trifle' from a list in the Eton Latin Grammar. A word of twenty-nine letters was created to mean 'meh'.

cards.title: The Paradox of Heterological
cards.story: Some words describe themselves: 'short' is short. Those that do not, like 'long', are called heterological. Now: is 'heterological' heterological? If yes, it describes itself, so it isn't. If no, it doesn't, so it is. Language eats its own tail.

cards.title: The Hidden Adjective Rule
cards.story: You would say 'a lovely little old green French whittling knife', never 'a French old green lovely little knife'. Native speakers follow a strict order: opinion, size, age, colour, origin, purpose. Almost nobody can recite it. Everyone obeys it.

cards.title: tick-tock
cards.story: Ping-pong, King Kong, tick-tock, sing-song, flip-flop: when we repeat a word with a vowel change, the order is almost always I, then A, then O. Nobody taught you this. Try saying 'tock-tick' and feel your tongue object.

cards.title: children
cards.hook: Plural twice, just to be sure.
cards.story: Old English cild had the plural cildru. Later speakers, forgetting that, added the other old plural ending, -en, so that children is a double plural. Brethren is the same. English has been told to clean this up and has not bothered.

cards.title: thou
cards.hook: English once had tu and aap.
cards.story: Thou was the intimate form, like Hindi tu, and you was the respectful one, like aap. Calling a stranger 'thou' could start a fight. English then dropped thou. So while thou sounds grand and ancient today, it was actually the casual one.

cards.title: octopus
cards.story: Octopus is Greek, not Latin, so the Latin-looking plural octopi is a false guess. Octopodes is the true Greek plural. In practice, octopuses is correct, and it should end the argument, but people will still correct you at dinner parties.

When Ray Tomlinson needed a symbol for his 1971 email system, he picked @. Other languages had fun naming it: monkey's tail in Dutch, snail in Italian, little dog in Russian, and strudel in Hebrew. English calls it 'at', which is typical.

cards.title: octothorpe
cards.story: Bell Labs engineers needed a name for the # on a new telephone keypad and came up with octothorpe: octo for its eight points, and thorpe for reasons now disputed. One story blames the athlete Jim Thorpe. Nobody knows for sure.

cards.title: interrobang
cards.hook: The punctuation that never caught on.
cards.story: In 1962 advertising man Martin Speckter proposed merging the question mark and the exclamation mark into one symbol for questions like 'You did what?!' He named it interrobang. The symbol flopped, though the need for it has never been greater.

cards.title: Gadsby
cards.hook: Fifty thousand words without an e.
cards.story: Ernest Wright wrote a novel of over 50,000 words without one letter e, tying down that key on his typewriter. It came out in 1939. Georges Perec's La Disparition later did the same in French, and Gilbert Adair translated it into English, also with no e.

cards.title: shibboleth
cards.story: In the Book of Judges, soldiers tested fugitives by making them say shibboleth. Those who said 'sibboleth' were killed: 42,000, the book says. A word for 'ear of grain' became the word for any small test of who belongs.

cards.title: literally
cards.story: Complaining about 'literally' meaning 'figuratively' is a modern hobby. But Dickens, Charlotte Brontë, Mark Twain and James Joyce all used it for emphasis. It has been going on for about 250 years, and the complaints have not, literally, stopped it.

cards.title: singular they
cards.story: Everyone should mind their own business. English has used 'they' for one person since about 1375, when it appeared in the poem William and the Werewolf. Shakespeare did it too. Style guides caught up more than six hundred years later.

cards.title: The Preposition Rule
cards.hook: A poet made this rule up.
cards.story: Never end a sentence with a preposition: that rule was popularised after John Dryden criticised Ben Jonson for doing it in 1672, by analogy with Latin. The quip about Churchill and 'up with which I will not put' is almost certainly invented too.

cards.title: The Surgeon of Crowthorne
cards.hook: Locked away, he helped write the OED.
cards.story: William Chester Minor, an American army surgeon, killed a stranger in London in 1872 and was confined to Broadmoor asylum. From his cell he sent tens of thousands of quotations to the Oxford English Dictionary. Its editor visited him for years.

cards.title: pastern
cards.story: In his 1755 dictionary, Samuel Johnson defined a pastern as the knee of a horse. It is part of the foot. When a lady asked how he had got it wrong, the great lexicographer said: 'Ignorance, madam, pure ignorance.' Rarely has a correction been so graceful.

cards.title: oats
cards.story: Johnson's dictionary defined oats as 'a grain, which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland appears to support the people'. Legend credits a Scottish lord with the reply: 'And where else will you find such horses, and such men?'

cards.title: lexicographer
cards.hook: How he defined his own job.
cards.story: Lexicographer, said Johnson, means 'a writer of dictionaries; a harmless drudge'. No dictionary writer has been so honest since. He spent nearly a decade defining more than 40,000 words, and it is a safe bet he enjoyed writing that one most of all.

cards.title: esquivalience
cards.story: The New Oxford American Dictionary of 2001 defined esquivalience as the wilful avoidance of official responsibilities. The word was fake, planted to catch copiers. Such trap entries are called mountweazels, after a fictitious woman in a 1975 encyclopedia.

cards.title: etaoin shrdlu
cards.story: Linotype keys were arranged by how often letters appear. When a typesetter made an error, they would run a finger down the first two columns to fill the line, producing etaoin shrdlu. Sometimes it slipped past the proofreaders and appeared in the news.

cards.title: Semantic Satiation
cards.story: Repeat a word aloud and it gradually stops meaning anything. Leon Jakobovits James named this semantic satiation in 1962. Try it with 'spoon'. The brain gets tired of a word and stops answering.

cards.title: Desert Desert
cards.story: The Sahara Desert means 'Desert Desert': sahra is Arabic for desert. River Avon means 'River River', since afon is Welsh for river. The Gobi Desert and, in Indian restaurants, naan bread (naan means bread) are running the same joke.

cards.title: I
cards.story: Old English ic shrank to i, and a lone letter on a crowded page could get lost. Scribes seem to have made it taller so it would not vanish. Nobody has proved that ego was the reason, but English is a rare language that capitalises 'I' and not 'you'.

cards.title: The Cupertino Effect
cards.story: Early spellcheckers, given 'cooperation' without a hyphen, suggested Cupertino, the California town. It got into official papers at NATO, the UN and the EU. One NATO text reported that 'the Cupertino with our Italian comrades proved to be very fruitful'.

cards.title: I Before E
cards.story: 'I before E, except after C' looks like a rule and behaves like a rumour. Weird, seize, science, species, heist and their all ignore it. Even efficient, ancient and society break it after the c. Perhaps the oddest word in this sentence is 'rule'.

cards.title: gruntled
cards.story: P. G. Wodehouse wrote of a man who, 'if not actually disgruntled', was 'far from being gruntled'. English has many one-sided pairs: ruthless without ruth (pity), uncouth without couth, unkempt without kempt. We lost the positive and kept the complaint.

cards.title: Chiasmus
cards.hook: The sentence that folds in half.
cards.story: 'Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country.' Kennedy's famous line is chiasmus: A then B, then B then A, the sentence folding back on itself. The Greek name means 'marked with an X', the shape of the crossing.
cards.try: Eat to live, do not live to eat.

cards.title: Litotes
cards.story: 'Not bad', 'no small feat', 'she is not unintelligent'. Litotes affirms something by denying its opposite, and so makes a claim quietly. Old English poets adored it. In an exam passage, 'not unconvincing' is grudging approval, not praise.
cards.try: It was no mean achievement for a first-year student.

cards.title: Zeugma
cards.story: Dickens wrote that Miss Bolo 'went straight home, in a flood of tears and a sedan chair'. One word, 'in', does two different jobs, and that is zeugma. The trick lies in the second meaning, which should surprise and slightly embarrass the first.
cards.try: He lost his keys, his temper and, by evening, his job.

cards.title: Anaphora
cards.hook: The drumbeat at the start of lines.
cards.story: 'We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields.' Churchill's repetition at the start of each clause is anaphora. It builds weight until the listener feels a kind of inevitability.
cards.try: Every day, every hour, every minute, the deadline came closer.

cards.title: Epistrophe
cards.story: Lincoln ended the Gettysburg Address with 'government of the people, by the people, for the people'. Epistrophe repeats at the end of phrases, and the ear waits for the final word. It is how great speeches get their rhythm.
cards.try: When the going got tough, we worked. When the money ran out, we worked.

cards.title: Antithesis
cards.story: 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.' Antithesis puts contrasting ideas in matching shapes, so the contrast does the arguing. Dickens's 'best of times, worst of times' does the same. The balance makes it sound like a truth.
cards.try: Speech is silver; silence is golden.

cards.title: The Periodic Sentence
cards.hook: The point is saved until last.
cards.story: A periodic sentence holds its main idea until the very end, so you must keep reading to understand. 'Through the rain, past the gates, despite every warning, he came.' The reader leans forward. Use it sparingly; readers only lean so far.
cards.try: After years of waiting, planning and doubt, she finally resigned.

cards.title: The Cumulative Sentence
cards.hook: Start with the point, then add.
cards.story: The reverse of the periodic sentence. It states the main idea first, then adds details, each one a small surprise: 'She left, quietly, at dawn, without her coat, without looking back.' CAT passages often hide their real claim in the add-ons.
cards.try: He nodded, slowly, as if the answer were being read to him from far away.

cards.title: Understatement
cards.hook: Saying much less than you mean.
cards.story: Apollo 13's oxygen tank exploded, and the crew reported: 'Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here.' That is understatement: the calm voice makes the danger feel larger. The film changed it to 'we have a problem', which is rather less calm.
cards.try: The Titanic's maiden voyage was somewhat disappointing.

cards.title: Parallelism
cards.story: 'To err is human; to forgive, divine.' Parallel grammar makes ideas feel equal and connected. Break the pattern and the sentence limps: 'She likes reading, to swim, and her dog.' Good para-jumble answers often follow this alignment.
cards.try: She came to argue, to listen and to learn.

cards.title: Tricolon
cards.story: Churchill actually offered 'blood, toil, tears and sweat': four things. The world remembered 'blood, sweat and tears', because three feels complete. That three-part rhythm is tricolon, and it even edits history's greatest speeches.
cards.try: Veni, vidi, vici: I came, I saw, I conquered.

cards.title: Asyndeton
cards.story: Caesar's 'I came, I saw, I conquered' has no 'and' in it. Leaving out the conjunctions makes actions feel sudden, rapid and decisive. Add the 'and' back and you hear a bored child reading a shopping list.
cards.try: He arrived, ate, complained, left.

cards.title: Polysyndeton
cards.story: 'And God said, Let there be light: and there was light.' The Book of Genesis keeps adding 'and' to create a slow, stately, unstoppable rhythm. Hemingway borrowed this trick for his long, piling-up sentences. It is the opposite of asyndeton.
cards.try: We ran and we fell and we rose and we ran again.

cards.title: Metonymy
cards.story: 'Delhi announced a new policy', 'the pen is mightier than the sword', 'the Crown prosecuted'. Metonymy replaces a thing with something closely associated with it. Delhi, the city, stands in for the people in charge.
cards.try: The bench refused the bail plea.

cards.title: Synecdoche
cards.hook: A part stands for the whole.
cards.story: 'All hands on deck.' The captain needs the whole sailor, not just the hands. Synecdoche uses a part to mean the whole, or the reverse: 'India won the match' means eleven people did. Once you spot it, every headline looks different.
cards.try: We need a few more heads at the meeting.

cards.title: Oxymoron
cards.hook: The word itself is a joke.
cards.story: Oxymoron is built from Greek oxys, sharp, and moros, dull. So the word for 'two contradictory words put together' is itself two contradictory words put together. Few terms in any language are so completely what they describe.
cards.try: Bittersweet, deafening silence, and a definite maybe.

cards.title: Paradox
cards.hook: A contradiction that turns out true.
cards.story: Oscar Wilde had a character say: 'I can resist everything except temptation.' A paradox seems to contradict itself while quietly telling the truth. Wilde's lines repay a second reading, and so do the paradoxes in reading passages.
cards.try: The more you learn, the less you know.

cards.title: Hyperbole
cards.story: 'I have told you a million times.' Hyperbole knowingly overstates something to make a point. Nobody counts the million. In reading passages, a writer's hyperbole often signals strong feeling, and a sudden restraint signals that the real point is close.
cards.try: This bag weighs a ton and I have walked a thousand miles.

cards.title: Irony
cards.story: In 1729, Jonathan Swift proposed that the poor of Ireland could solve their troubles by selling their babies as food. He meant the exact opposite: that the English were already devouring Ireland. Irony says one thing while meaning something else entirely.

cards.title: The Rhetorical Question
cards.story: Shylock asks, 'If you prick us, do we not bleed?' He is not asking. A rhetorical question expects no answer, and the missing answer is the argument. If a CAT passage asks one, the author has already decided what you should think.
cards.try: Who, after all, would argue against clean water?

cards.title: Alliteration
cards.story: Repeating the opening consonant sound makes words stick together in the memory. Headlines love it, poets use it and brands have built empires on it: Coca-Cola, Krispy Kreme. Old English poetry was built almost entirely on alliteration, not on rhyme.
cards.try: The tired teacher took the train.

cards.title: Onomatopoeia
cards.story: Buzz, hiss, plop, crackle: onomatopoeia means 'name-making', for words formed from sounds. Languages disagree about the sounds: English dogs say woof, Hindi dogs say bhau-bhau, Japanese dogs say wan-wan. Everybody hears the same dog differently.
cards.try: Rain pattered, the kettle hissed and the door creaked shut.

cards.title: Euphemism
cards.story: 'Passed away', 'let go', 'collateral damage': a euphemism replaces a harsh term with a gentle one. Greek eu means good, pheme means speech. The words say one thing and hide another, which is why a careful reader always asks what is being hidden.
cards.try: The company is right-sizing its workforce.

cards.title: Apophasis
cards.story: 'I won't mention his debts, or his lies.' Now you have. Apophasis raises a subject by pretending not to. Mark Antony does it brilliantly: 'I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him', and then spends the whole speech praising Caesar.
cards.try: I need not remind you of last year's results.

cards.title: Anadiplosis
cards.story: 'Fear leads to anger. Anger leads to hate. Hate leads to suffering.' Yoda's warning ends each clause on the word that begins the next. That is anadiplosis, and it makes an argument feel like a chain, where each link drags in the next.
cards.try: Strength brings confidence. Confidence brings risk. Risk brings ruin.

cards.title: Hendiadys
cards.story: 'Nice and warm' is not really two things: it means nicely warm. Hendiadys splits one idea into two joined words. Shakespeare's 'sound and fury' does the job: the fury is the sound, and the sound is the fury. Prose gains body from it.
cards.try: The report was good and thorough.

cards.title: Aposiopesis
cards.story: King Lear, beside himself with rage: 'I will do such things... what they are, yet I know not.' Aposiopesis is the sudden breaking off of a sentence, as if feeling had choked the words. The silence works harder than anything he could have said.
cards.try: If you say that to her one more time, I swear I will...

cards.title: Tmesis
cards.story: Eliza Doolittle sings 'abso-bloomin-lutely' in My Fair Lady, and that is tmesis: pushing another word right into the middle of a word. Greek tmesis means a cutting. English speakers do it almost entirely to show how strongly they feel.
cards.try: That is fan-flipping-tastic news.

cards.title: The Transferred Epithet
cards.hook: The night that could not sleep.
cards.story: 'She had a sleepless night.' The night did not sleep; she did. Moving an adjective to the wrong noun is a transferred epithet, and good writers love it. P. G. Wodehouse: 'I balanced a thoughtful lump of sugar on the teaspoon.' The lump did no thinking.
cards.try: He drove home with a nervous cigarette between his fingers.

cards.title: Bathos
cards.story: Alexander Pope gave English this word for the sudden drop from grand to trivial. He did it himself: 'Here thou, great Anna! whom three realms obey, dost sometimes counsel take, and sometimes tea.' The Queen, her politics, and then teatime.
cards.try: He lost his home, his family, and his favourite pen.

cards.title: Hypophora
cards.story: 'What is the answer to poverty? Education.' Hypophora asks a question and immediately answers it, taking control of the conversation. It is a favourite of essayists and TED speakers, and in a CAT passage it usually hands you the author's main claim.
cards.try: Why does this matter? Because the poor pay first.

cards.title: Polyptoton
cards.hook: The same root, in different clothes.
cards.story: 'Judge not, that ye be not judged.' The same word returns in a different form. Polyptoton gives an argument a kind of moral neatness, and Shakespeare loved it. Once you learn the name, you will start to find it in every advertising slogan.
cards.try: Who will watch the watchers?

cards.title: Dead Metaphor
cards.story: The leg of a table. The foot of a hill. The mouth of a river. Each began as a bold image, and each has died into plain speech. So have 'bottleneck' and 'head of state'. Much of the language you use is retired metaphor.

cards.title: Antanaclasis
cards.story: 'We must all hang together, or assuredly we shall all hang separately', Benjamin Franklin supposedly said at the signing of the Declaration of Independence. The word 'hang' shifts from stand together to the gallows in one sentence. That is antanaclasis.
cards.try: If you aren't fired with enthusiasm, you will be fired with enthusiasm.

cards.title: The Short Sentence
cards.story: A long sentence builds a little momentum and carries the reader along through clauses and qualifications and afterthoughts. Then a short one stops it. Dead. Good writers alternate. Bad writers do one or the other, and you stop reading.

cards.title: Chekhov's Gun
cards.story: Chekhov told a writer that if a loaded gun is on the wall in the first act, it must go off later. Everything placed in a story is a promise. In a reading passage too, every example is there for a reason: ask what job it is doing.

cards.title: The However Hinge
cards.hook: The paragraph turns on one word.
cards.story: Everything before 'however' is usually the scenery. Everything after is the point. Writers set up a view, hold it up for you, then swing on that hinge. When you see 'however' in a CAT passage, slow down: the author is about to say what they really think.

cards.title: Adjectives Are Spies
cards.hook: The opinion is in the adjectives.
cards.story: A writer can claim to be neutral and still reveal everything. 'The so-called reform', 'a merely technical change', 'his much-admired theory'. Underline the adjectives and adverbs. That is where the author's hidden opinion is smuggled in.

cards.title: Beware the Extreme Word
cards.story: In CAT options, words like always, never, only, entirely and all are danger signals, because passages rarely make claims that strong. They are not automatically wrong. But the option must be as strong as the passage is. Usually it is not.

cards.title: Not Unconvincing
cards.story: 'The argument is not unconvincing.' Two negatives do not quite cancel. The phrase is litotes: careful, lukewarm, slightly reluctant approval. If a CAT option translates it as 'persuasive' or 'compelling', it has turned a shrug into a standing ovation.
cards.try: His defence of the plan was not unconvincing.

cards.title: The Concession Trick
cards.story: Admittedly, true, of course, to be sure, granted: these words concede a point to the other side. Authors do it to seem fair, just before delivering the real blow. The claim that follows is the author's own. The concession is only the run-up.
cards.try: Admittedly the data are thin, but the pattern is hard to ignore.

cards.title: Reading the Tone
cards.story: Tone is rarely stated. It leaks through word choice. Is a plan 'bold' or 'reckless'? A crowd 'spirited' or 'unruly'? CAT's correct tone options tend to be measured, such as 'cautiously optimistic'. Extreme ones like 'vitriolic' are usually wrong.

cards.title: True but Not the Answer
cards.hook: A fact can still be the wrong option.
cards.story: The meanest trap in main-idea questions is the option that is perfectly true according to the passage and still wrong. It describes one paragraph, not the whole passage. Ask 'Does this cover everything the author is doing?' True is not enough.

cards.title: Too Big for the Passage
cards.story: If the passage discusses Indian agriculture, an option about 'the future of humanity' has wandered off. The right answer should be the same size as the passage: not a paragraph's detail, not a philosophy of everything. Size is half the test.

cards.title: The Echo Trap
cards.hook: Familiar words can be a trick.
cards.story: Examiners love an option that reuses the passage's exact words while twisting what they meant. It feels right because you recognise the phrasing. Good answers usually paraphrase. Bad answers often echo. Familiar wording is a warning, not a reward.

cards.title: Scare Quotes
cards.story: When a writer puts a single word in quotation marks, as in the 'experts' said or the 'reform' failed, they are keeping the word at arm's length. Those quotation marks are a raised eyebrow. They tell you the writer does not believe it.
cards.try: The 'reform' left every old rule in place.

cards.title: Whose Voice Is It?
cards.hook: Most mistakes are about who's talking.
cards.story: Critics argue, some believe, it has been said, many historians hold. Authors constantly report views they do not share. A huge share of wrong answers come from crediting the author with someone else's opinion. Keep asking: who is talking right now?

cards.title: Inference Means a Small Step
cards.hook: An inference is a small step.
cards.story: An inference question asks only what must be true, given the passage. Not what is likely, and not what you happen to know about the world. If your answer needs one extra assumption from outside the passage, you have jumped too far.

cards.title: Signal Words Are Road Signs
cards.story: Moreover and furthermore say keep going straight. But, however and yet say turn. Therefore and thus say you have arrived. Underline them on your first read, and a dense passage becomes a road map, with every turn marked.

cards.title: Many Believe
cards.hook: The author is about to disagree.
cards.story: When a writer opens with 'Many believe', 'It is widely thought' or 'Conventional wisdom says', you are usually looking at a target being set up. Nobody writes an article to agree with the crowd. The next sentences will, almost certainly, knock it down.

cards.title: The Hedging Scale
cards.story: Perhaps, may, might, tends to, suggests: these words show exactly how sure the author is. An option that turns 'may contribute' into 'causes' has smuggled in confidence that the author never had. Check strength first, and content second.

cards.title: Ask What the Example Is Doing
cards.story: In a function question, the answer is never what the example says. It is what the example is for. Ask why the author brought it up: to prove a claim, to contrast, to concede, to illustrate. Examples are employees. Ask what their job is.

cards.title: The Assumption Test
cards.story: To check if something is an assumption, flip it: make it false, then see whether the argument collapses. If it does, you have found the hidden plank the whole argument stands on. If nothing breaks, it was decoration. The trick almost never fails.

cards.title: Attack the Bridge
cards.hook: Hit the link, not the claim.
cards.story: An argument has a premise and a conclusion, joined by a bridge of reasoning. To weaken it, do not simply deny the conclusion. Attack the bridge. Ask what would have to be true for the evidence to lead to the conclusion. That is where it breaks.

cards.title: Spot the Para Jumble Opener
cards.hook: The first sentence has no baggage.
cards.story: A sentence starting with 'This', 'However', 'Such', or a pronoun almost never opens a para jumble: it needs something before it. Find the sentence that stands alone and introduces a topic, and the chain of this, it and they will assemble itself.

cards.title: The Last Two Options
cards.story: You are down to two. Read them against each other and find the words that differ. That difference is the question the examiner is really asking. Go back to the passage for that one difference only. The wrong option is usually wrong in a single word.

cards.title: Best Means Least Wrong
cards.hook: You are not looking for perfect.
cards.story: CAT asks for the best option. That means the option that fits better than the others, not a perfect one. Students lose time hunting for an answer with no flaws. Choose the one with the smallest flaw, and move on.

cards.title: Cause and Effect, Reversed
cards.story: A passage says poverty causes poor health. An option says poor health causes poverty. Same words, opposite direction. This is one of the cleanest traps in the exam. Before you accept any causal option, check which way the arrow points.

cards.title: Linked Is Not Caused
cards.story: Passage: higher income is associated with longer life. Option: higher income makes you live longer. The option has upgraded a link to a cause. Words like associated, correlated and linked never promise causation. Examiners rely on you forgetting that.

cards.title: The Scope Shift
cards.hook: One small word changes the set.
cards.story: Watch the fences around every claim. Passage: 'Some urban students.' Option: 'Students.' Passage: 'In the 1990s.' Option: 'Today.' Scope shifts change who, where or when by one small word, and they feel right because the rest is accurate.

cards.title: The Brackets Speak
cards.hook: The aside often holds the opinion.
cards.story: An author's brackets are often the most honest part of the paragraph. A little 'it must be said' or 'as ever' or 'to the surprise of no one' can carry more attitude than the main sentence. Authors whisper their real opinions in the margins.

cards.title: Once Thought
cards.hook: The past tense is a warning.
cards.story: 'Scientists once believed', 'It was long assumed', 'For decades, experts held'. The past tense is the first clue. The writer is about to tell you that the old idea is wrong. The moment you see 'once believed', look for what replaced it.

cards.title: The Word Even
cards.story: 'Even experts were confused.' That 'even' tells you that experts are not usually confused. 'Even' exposes what the author expected the world to be like. Tiny words reveal attitudes that longer sentences work hard to hide.

cards.title: Words of Distrust
cards.story: Ostensibly, purportedly, supposedly, allegedly, so-called. These are the words an author uses when quietly refusing to believe what they are reporting. If you see one, the passage is disagreeing, even if its tone stays polite.
cards.try: The scheme was ostensibly voluntary.

cards.title: Mistakes Were Made
cards.story: 'Mistakes were made.' The passive voice removes the person responsible, which is why politicians love it. In reading passages, ask who did the action. When the author hides the doer, it may be a fact they prefer not to dwell on.

cards.title: Although Tells You What Matters
cards.hook: The main clause has the weight.
cards.story: 'Although the film made money, the critics hated it.' The writer wants you to focus on the critics. Switch the clauses and the emphasis flips. The information after 'although' is what the author is setting aside. The main clause is the message.

cards.title: Not X but Y
cards.hook: Y is the author's real view.
cards.story: 'The crisis was caused not by greed but by fear.' Whenever you see this pattern, the author has just given you their thesis. Y is the claim. X is the rejected alternative. Many correct answers are simply Y, written in different words.

cards.title: Indeed Turns It Up
cards.story: Indeed is a volume knob. 'The plan was costly. Indeed, it nearly bankrupted the city.' It signals that the next point goes further than the previous one, in the same direction. If 'however' is a U-turn, 'indeed' is a foot on the accelerator.

cards.title: Your Eyes Don't Glide
cards.story: Your eyes feel like they glide along a line. They do not. They jump in short hops called saccades, taking in text only during stops lasting a fraction of a second. Roughly one jump in eight goes backwards. Reading is a stop-start miracle.

cards.title: Title Every Paragraph
cards.story: After each paragraph, write five words in the margin saying what it did: 'introduces rival theory', 'gives counter-example'. You are building a map of the passage. Most CAT questions can then be answered by looking at the map, not the territory.

cards.title: The End of the Sentence
cards.hook: Writers save the best for last.
cards.story: English places its weight at the end of a sentence. The start carries what you already know; the end delivers the new information. Read the last few words of a long sentence carefully: that is usually where the writer wants you to look.

cards.title: Count the Negatives
cards.hook: Treat them like plus and minus.
cards.story: 'It is not impossible that nobody disagreed.' When negatives pile up, treat each one as a minus sign and cancel them in pairs. Here it leaves 'It is possible that everyone agreed.' Examiners stack negatives because panicked readers do not count.
